title: Two ways to divide, cells with no job yet, and cells that die on time

summary.text: Your fingers began as a flat paddle, so some of your cells had to die on time. How does a body make a hand? In this lesson you will test which piece of a mint stem grows roots, and act out two ways cells divide with paper chromosomes.
summary.art: A tumbler of water on a window sill holding a pudina cutting with new white roots, beside a child's open hand with the fingers spread.

intro.hook: Cut a 6 centimetre piece from a pudina stem and stand it in water. In about a week it grows roots, and later it becomes a whole plant. The piece had no roots at all. So which cells made the new roots, and where in the stem were they waiting? Say what you think, and why.
intro.text: You will test this yourself in the Pudina Pieces Test, with four kinds of pieces. Before that, here is a second puzzle. Every cell in your body came from one first cell, by copying. Copies are the same as each other. So why are a brother and a sister from the same two parents not copies of each other? Both puzzles are about how cells divide, and about what a cell is still able to become.
intro.art: A child holding a short piece of pudina stem above a tumbler of water, looking closely at the place where two leaves join the stem.

outcomes: By the end I can say what mitosis does and what meiosis does, and how the cells they make are different.
By the end I can explain why egg and sperm cells carry half the chromosomes, and why two children of the same parents are not copies.
By the end I can say what a stem cell is, and how the stem cells of an early embryo differ from those in a grown body.
By the end I can explain what programmed cell death is, give three examples, and tell it apart from death by injury.
By the end I can run a fair test with cuttings, and say what it shows about where a plant keeps cells that can still divide.
By the end I can use doubling and halving to work out chromosome numbers and the number of possible egg cells.
By the end I can give two views on a question about cells that scientists have not settled.

terms.meaning: A chromosome is one long thread of DNA, wound up tight. DNA is the long molecule that holds a cell's instructions. A human body cell has 46 chromosomes.
terms.example: A garden pea plant has 14 chromosomes in each body cell, and a rice plant has 24.
terms.art: A cell with a round nucleus, and an arrow from the nucleus to a row of small X-shaped chromosomes.

terms.meaning: Your 46 chromosomes are 23 matching pairs. In each pair, one chromosome came from your mother and one from your father. The two carry the same kinds of instructions, but often different versions.
terms.example: Both chromosomes of one pair may carry instructions for the ear lobe. One version may say 'attached' and the other 'free'.
terms.art: Two chromosomes of the same length side by side, one red and one blue, with matching bands in slightly different shades.

terms.meaning: Mitosis is cell division that makes copies. The cell copies every chromosome and divides once. The two new cells each have the full set, the same as the first cell.
terms.example: When a scraped knee heals, skin cells at the edge of the scrape divide by mitosis.
terms.art: One cell with four chromosomes becoming two cells, each with the same four chromosomes.

terms.meaning: Meiosis is the special division that makes egg cells and sperm cells. The cell copies every chromosome once and then divides twice. The new cells have half the set, and no two are the same.
terms.example: In a hibiscus flower, meiosis happens inside the anthers, where pollen is made.
terms.art: One cell with four chromosomes becoming four smaller cells, each with two chromosomes in different colour mixes.

terms.meaning: A sex cell is a cell with half the chromosomes, made to join with another sex cell. Egg cells and sperm cells are sex cells. Scientists also call them gametes.
terms.example: A human egg cell has 23 chromosomes, and so has a human sperm cell.
terms.art: A large round egg cell beside a tiny sperm cell with a long tail, each labelled 23.

terms.meaning: Fertilisation is the joining of an egg cell and a sperm cell into one cell. That one cell has the full number of chromosomes again.
terms.example: 23 chromosomes from the egg and 23 from the sperm make the 46 of a fertilised human egg.
terms.art: A sperm cell entering an egg cell, with the sum 23 + 23 = 46 written beside it.

terms.meaning: Crossing over is a swap of matching pieces between the two chromosomes of a pair. It happens early in meiosis, and it mixes the mother's and father's versions on one chromosome.
terms.example: After crossing over, one chromosome can carry your grandmother's version at one end and your grandfather's at the other.
terms.art: A red and a blue chromosome lying crossed, then separate again with their tips exchanged.

terms.meaning: A specialised cell is a cell that has taken on one job, and has the shape and parts for that job.
terms.example: A red blood cell carries oxygen. A nerve cell carries signals. A root hair cell takes in water.
terms.art: A red blood cell, a long nerve cell and a root hair cell drawn side by side.

terms.meaning: A stem cell is a cell that has not taken a job yet. When she divides, she can make another stem cell and also a cell that goes on to specialise.
terms.example: Blood stem cells in your bone marrow make every kind of blood cell, every day of your life.
terms.art: One round cell dividing into two, with one daughter staying round and the other changing into a red blood cell.

terms.meaning: An embryonic stem cell is a stem cell from an embryo a few days old. An embryo is a living being at the earliest stage of growing. These cells can become every kind of cell in the body.
terms.example: In a five-day-old embryo, a small group of inner cells will make the whole body.
terms.art: A hollow ball of cells cut open to show a small cluster of cells inside, with arrows to skin, nerve, muscle and blood cells.

terms.meaning: An adult stem cell is a stem cell in a body that is already formed, in a child or a grown-up. She can make only the few kinds of cell that her own part of the body needs.
terms.example: A skin stem cell makes new skin cells. She does not make blood or bone.
terms.art: A layer of skin in cross-section with one cell in the bottom layer highlighted and new cells moving upward from it.

terms.meaning: Bone marrow is the soft tissue inside large bones. Blood stem cells live there and make new blood cells.
terms.example: The marrow in your hip bones, ribs and backbone makes about two million red blood cells every second.
terms.art: A bone cut lengthwise to show the soft red marrow inside, with tiny blood cells leaving it.

terms.meaning: A node is the place on a plant stem where a leaf joins. A node holds a tiny bud, and cells that can start dividing again.
terms.example: On a pudina stem, the nodes are the small bumps where each pair of leaves is attached.
terms.art: A pudina stem with one node circled, showing two leaves and two tiny buds at the joint.

terms.meaning: Programmed cell death is the death of a cell by plan. The cell gets a signal and takes herself apart in a tidy way. The best-known kind in animals is called apoptosis (say: a-pop-TOE-sis).
terms.example: The cells between your fingers died this way before you were born, and that separated your fingers.
terms.art: A hand-shaped paddle with dotted patches between the finger shapes, and beside it a hand with separate fingers.

terms.meaning: Necrosis is the death of cells by injury, such as a burn, a crush or a loss of blood supply. The cells swell and burst, and the place becomes red and sore.
terms.example: The skin under a bad burn dies by necrosis. Nobody planned it, and the body has to clean it up.
terms.art: A swollen cell bursting open with its contents leaking, beside neighbouring cells that look irritated.

terms.meaning: A checkpoint is a pause in cell division. The cell checks that a step is finished before she goes on to the next step.
terms.example: A dividing cell waits until every chromosome is held by threads from both sides. Only then does she pull the copies apart.
terms.art: Chromosomes lined up across the middle of a cell with one still unattached, and a small 'wait' sign above the cell.

explanations.concept: Two ways to divide: mitosis and meiosis
explanations.definition: Mitosis makes two cells that each have the full set of chromosomes, the same as the first cell. Meiosis makes cells with half the set, and each one is different.
explanations.description: Almost every division in your body is mitosis. The cell copies all 46 chromosomes. The copies line up one by one across the middle, and one copy of each goes to each side. Then the cell divides once. Both new cells have 46 chromosomes, with the same instructions. That is what a body needs for growing and mending: more cells of the same kind. Meiosis happens in only one place, the organs that make egg cells or sperm cells. It starts the same way, by copying every chromosome once. Then two things are different. First, the chromosomes do not line up one by one. Each chromosome finds its matching partner, and the pairs line up together. Second, the cell divides twice. The first division separates the partners. The second division separates the copies. The result is four cells with 23 chromosomes each. This is the simple picture. One more detail matters. In a testis, all four cells become sperm. In an ovary, the divisions are unequal, so there is one large egg cell and two or three tiny cells that break down.
examples: A fertilised egg divides by mitosis to make the trillions of cells of a body.
A moong root gets longer because cells at its tip divide by mitosis.
In a pumpkin flower, meiosis in the anthers leads to pollen, and meiosis in the ovules leads to egg cells.
In the Two Dances activity, paper chromosomes show both divisions side by side.
explanations.art: Two columns: on the left one cell becoming two identical cells, on the right one cell becoming four smaller cells with half as many chromosomes each.

explanations.concept: Why egg and sperm cells must have half
explanations.definition: An egg cell and a sperm cell join to start a new life. Each must bring half the chromosomes, so that the fertilised egg has the full number and not double.
explanations.description: Think what would happen without the halving. A human egg with 46 chromosomes would join a sperm with 46. The child would have 92 in every cell. The grandchild would have 184, and the number would double in every generation. Cells do not work with a doubled set like that, and a human embryo with 92 does not live. So the number must be halved before it is added together again. But the halving has to be exact. A sex cell does not get any 23 chromosomes. She gets one chromosome from each of the 23 matching pairs. That way no kind of instruction is missing and none is doubled. This is why the pairs line up as partners in meiosis. Lining up as partners is how the cell makes sure that one of each pair goes each way. Some plants do live well with doubled sets. Bread wheat has six sets of chromosomes. Their meiosis still halves the number exactly.
examples: A pea plant has 14 chromosomes. A pea egg cell has 7, and a sperm cell inside a pollen grain has 7. Together they make 14 again.
In the Double Trouble activity, a katori of 14 seeds becomes 28, then 56, when nothing is halved.
A rice plant has 24 chromosomes in body cells and 12 in sex cells.
explanations.art: A family tree of katoris: with no halving the katoris hold 14, 28 and 56 seeds, and with halving every katori holds 14.

explanations.concept: The shuffle: why no two egg cells are alike
explanations.definition: In meiosis, each matching pair of chromosomes is shared out by chance, and the partners first swap pieces. So every egg cell and every sperm cell carries a different mix.
explanations.description: Your mother has 23 pairs of chromosomes. In each pair, one came from her mother and one from her father. When she makes an egg cell, the egg gets one chromosome from each pair. Which one it gets is chance, and each pair is shared out separately. With one pair there are 2 possible eggs. With two pairs there are 4, and with three pairs there are 8. The number doubles with every pair. With 23 pairs it comes to 8,388,608 different eggs. A father can make as many different sperm. So the same two parents could have more than 70 trillion different children, before any swapping is counted. And there is swapping. Early in meiosis the two partners lie side by side and exchange matching pieces. This is called crossing over. After it, a single chromosome is part grandmother's and part grandfather's. In 1931 Harriet Creighton and Barbara McClintock proved, with maize plants, that the chromosomes really do exchange pieces. So a brother and a sister are not copies. Each grew from a different egg and a different sperm. Identical twins are the exception, because they grew from one fertilised egg that split in two.
examples: In the Shuffle Test, three coins stand for three pairs of chromosomes, and 24 tosses give up to 8 different egg cells.
Two sisters share about half of their DNA on average, but never exactly the same half.
You did not get exactly one quarter of your DNA from each grandparent. The shuffle gives a little more from some and a little less from others.
explanations.art: A mother's three pairs of chromosomes, each pair with one red and one blue chromosome, and below them eight small egg cells showing all eight colour combinations.

explanations.concept: Egg cells wait, and sperm cells are made every day
explanations.definition: A girl's egg cells begin meiosis before she is born, and then they pause for years. A boy's body starts meiosis when he is about 11 to 14, and after that makes sperm every day.
explanations.description: A baby girl is born with all her egg cells, about one to two million of them. Each has already started meiosis and stopped part of the way through. They wait like that through her whole childhood. When she is grown, usually one egg cell each month carries on. The egg finishes the last step of meiosis only if a sperm cell enters her. So the egg cell that became you began to form inside your mother before your mother was born. A man's body works differently. From the early teens, stem cells in the testes keep dividing. Their daughter cells go through meiosis, and it takes about ten weeks to make a sperm cell. Many millions are finished every day. Sperm cells also decide one more thing. In 1905 Nettie Stevens studied mealworm beetles and found two kinds of sperm, one with a large chromosome and one with a small one. Eggs fertilised by the small-chromosome kind became males. Humans are similar: an egg always carries an X chromosome, and a sperm carries an X or a Y.
examples: A woman of 35 releases an egg cell that has been paused in meiosis for more than 35 years.
Of the million or more egg cells a girl is born with, only about 400 are ever released.
Nettie Stevens saw the two kinds of sperm through her microscope at Bryn Mawr College in the United States.
explanations.art: A timeline of a woman's life from before birth to adulthood, with an egg cell marked 'paused' along most of it, beside a short ten-week timeline for a sperm cell.

explanations.definition: Sometimes two partner chromosomes fail to separate in meiosis. Then one sex cell gets an extra chromosome and another gets one too few.
explanations.description: A dividing cell is careful. She has a checkpoint: she waits until every chromosome is held by threads from both sides before she pulls. Even so, a pair sometimes goes to the same side together. If that sex cell is fertilised, every cell of the new embryo has 47 chromosomes, or 45. Most such embryos stop growing very early, often before the mother knows she is pregnant. With some chromosomes the embryo can live and grow. A person with three copies of chromosome 21 has Down syndrome. People with Down syndrome usually learn more slowly and often have heart or eye problems that doctors can treat. They go to school, work, and live full lives. In 1958, in Paris, Marthe Gautier grew cells from children with Down syndrome and was the first to see the extra chromosome. The paper about it put a male colleague's name first, and for fifty years he got most of the credit. Unequal sharing is more common in egg cells that have waited longer. One likely reason is that the links holding the paired chromosomes together weaken over the years of waiting.
examples: In the Blind Share challenge, you design a way to share pairs with no mistakes while blindfolded, and compare it with the cell's way.
About 1 baby in 700 to 1,000 is born with Down syndrome.
A cell with one unattached chromosome waits at the checkpoint, sometimes for hours.
explanations.art: A dividing cell in which one pair of chromosomes is moving to the same side together while all the other pairs separate.

explanations.concept: Stem cells: cells that have not taken a job yet
explanations.definition: A stem cell is a cell that can do two things when she divides: make another stem cell, and make a cell that goes on to specialise.
explanations.description: Most cells in your body are specialised. A red blood cell carries oxygen and will never be anything else. A stem cell is different, because she has not specialised. When she divides, one daughter can stay a stem cell, so the supply never runs out. The other daughter goes on to become a working cell. It is often said that stem cells can become any cell. That is true only for the earliest ones. A fertilised egg, and her first few daughter cells, can each make a whole body. A few days later the embryo is a hollow ball. A small group of inner cells will make every kind of cell in the body, more than 200 kinds. These are embryonic stem cells. Gail Martin gave them that name in 1981, when she grew them from mouse embryos. As the body forms, cells choose their paths, and the choices narrow. The stem cells left in a grown body are adult stem cells. Each kind makes only the cells of her own tissue. Blood stem cells make blood, and skin stem cells make skin.
examples: Blood stem cells were proved to exist in 1961 by James Till and Ernest McCulloch in Toronto, who counted the colonies of new blood cells in mice.
Stem cells at the bottom of tiny pits in your gut wall remake the whole gut lining every few days.
A plant keeps cells like these at every root tip, every shoot tip and every bud. Such a growing point is called a meristem.
explanations.art: A branching diagram: one cell at the top, a ball of cells below, then branches narrowing to blood, skin, nerve and muscle cells, with small round stem cells left beside the blood and skin branches.

explanations.concept: Stem cells at work in a grown body
explanations.definition: Adult stem cells replace the cells that a body uses up, such as blood cells, skin cells and gut lining cells. Doctors can move some of them from one person to another.
explanations.description: A red blood cell lasts about four months. Your body holds about 25 trillion of them, so about two million must be made every second. Blood stem cells in your bone marrow do this, without a break. Doctors use this in a bone marrow transplant. A person whose marrow is ill, for example with a blood cancer called leukaemia, is given blood stem cells from a healthy person. The new stem cells settle in the bones and make blood for the rest of that person's life. Hospitals in India, including Tata Memorial Hospital in Mumbai and Christian Medical College in Vellore, have done this since the 1980s. The clear front window of your eye, the cornea, has stem cells too. They sit in a ring at its edge. A splash of chuna (lime) in the eye can kill them, and then the cornea turns cloudy. Since 2001, doctors at L V Prasad Eye Institute in Hyderabad, led by Virender Sangwan with the scientist Geeta Vemuganti, have taken a tiny piece of that ring from the person's other eye and grown new surface from it. Many people have got their sight back this way. These are the stem cell treatments that are well proven: blood, skin for burns, and the surface of the eye. Many others are still being tested.
examples: After a blood donation, your bone marrow replaces the red cells in about four to eight weeks.
Skin grown from a burn patient's own skin stem cells can cover large burns.
A bone marrow donor's own marrow grows back within a few weeks.
explanations.art: A hip bone with marrow sending out red blood cells, beside an eye seen from the front with a ring of stem cells marked around the edge of the cornea.

explanations.concept: Can a specialised cell go back?
explanations.definition: Plant cells can often go back to dividing and build any part of the plant. Animal cells rarely do this by themselves, but scientists can make them go back.
explanations.description: In the Pudina Pieces Test, roots grow from a stem that had none. Some cells near the node were already part of a finished stem. When the stem is cut and stood in water, they start dividing again, and their daughters build a root tip. Plants can go much further. In 1958 Frederick Steward grew whole carrot plants from single cells of a carrot root, in a liquid that contained coconut water. In 1964 Sipra Guha and Satish Maheshwari at the University of Delhi grew small plants from the young pollen of datura flowers. Those plants had only half the usual chromosomes, because pollen is made by meiosis. Most animals, including humans, do less of this. A house gecko regrows a lost tail. A flatworm called a planarian can be cut into many pieces, and each piece regrows a whole worm, because stem cells are spread all through their body. A human regrows liver, skin and blood, but not an arm. For a long time people thought an animal cell that had specialised could never go back. In 2006 Shinya Yamanaka and Kazutoshi Takahashi in Kyoto switched on just four genes in mouse skin cells. The skin cells turned into cells very like embryonic stem cells. So the instructions for every job are still there in a specialised cell. They are closed, not lost.
examples: A potato piece with an 'eye' grows a whole plant, because the eye is a bud with dividing cells.
If two thirds of a human liver is removed, the rest grows back to full size in a few weeks.
A gecko's new tail has a rod of cartilage inside and no new bones, so it is a repair and not an exact copy.
explanations.art: A pudina cutting in water with roots growing from a node, a carrot plant growing from a single cell in a flask, and a gecko with a shorter new tail.

explanations.concept: Programmed cell death: cells that die on time
explanations.definition: Programmed cell death is the planned death of a cell. The cell receives a signal, or senses damage inside herself, and takes herself apart neatly. In animals the main kind is called apoptosis.
explanations.description: A cell that dies by injury swells and bursts. Her contents spill out and irritate the cells around her, and the place becomes red and sore. That is necrosis. Apoptosis is very different. The cell shrinks. She cuts her own DNA into pieces and packs everything into small sealed parcels. Cleaner cells nearby swallow the parcels and reuse the material. Nothing spills, and nothing gets sore. Bodies use this in three ways. The first is shaping. Your hand began as a flat paddle. Finger bones formed inside it, and between about the sixth and eighth week the cells between them died, which freed the fingers. A tadpole's tail goes the same way when they become a frog. The second is choosing. A growing brain makes far more nerve cells than it keeps. In many parts, about half of them die, mostly those that did not link up well with others. Viktor Hamburger and Rita Levi-Montalcini first counted such deaths in chick embryos in 1949. The third is safety. A cell whose DNA is damaged beyond repair kills herself, and so does a cell taken over by a virus. This stops many cancers before they start. Plants use planned death too, with their own machinery. The cells that become a plant's water pipes build thick walls, then die and empty themselves, so that water can flow through.
examples: After a sunburn, skin peels because skin cells with badly damaged DNA have died by plan.
A duck keeps webbed feet because a signal blocker in the duck embryo's foot stops the cells between the toes from dying.
In the Dead on Purpose Hunt, you find hair, nails, wood, cotton and coir, all made of cells that finished their work by dying.
explanations.art: On the left a cell swelling and bursting; on the right a cell shrinking into small sealed parcels that a cleaner cell is swallowing.

explanations.concept: Why would a cell die for others?
explanations.definition: In a body, a cell that dies by plan protects cells that carry the same instructions. Why single-celled beings also have programmed death is still argued about.
explanations.description: In a body, the answer is fairly clear. All the cells of a body come from one fertilised egg and carry the same instructions. Only the egg and sperm cells pass those instructions to the next generation. So when a damaged skin cell dies, the instructions she carried still go on, through the body she protected. But programmed death is also found in beings that are a single cell. That is harder to explain, and scientists argue about it. The death machinery is also oddly placed. In animal cells, one main death signal is a protein let out by the mitochondria, the parts that release energy from food. Xiaodong Wang's laboratory found this in 1996. Mitochondria were once free-living bacteria, as Lynn Margulis argued in 1967. Why the death switch sits with them is not known.
examples: A bacterium attacked by a virus sometimes destroys herself before the virus can multiply, which protects her sister cells nearby.
Old yeast cells in a crowded colony can die in a tidy, programmed way.

perspectives.who: Biologists who study bacteria and their viruses
perspectives.explanation: A single cell who dies when a virus infects her saves her neighbours. Those neighbours are her sisters, with the same instructions. So her death keeps her own instructions going.
Much of what looks like planned death in single cells may be a breakdown, or a side effect of machinery that does other jobs. It may not have been shaped for the good of the neighbours.

A cell senses her own state and her neighbours, and decides. The colony or the body is the living being, and the cell acts as part of that being. Seen this way, the puzzle only comes from counting each cell as a separate life.

explanations.art: A colony of bacteria in which one infected cell has broken apart, with a ring of healthy sister cells around the gap.

agreed.text: Body cells divide by mitosis, and both new cells get a full copy of every chromosome.
agreed.evidence: Walther Flemming watched chromosomes being shared in dividing salamander cells in the 1870s and 1880s. Counts in thousands of kinds of cells since then agree.

agreed.text: Egg and sperm cells have half the chromosomes of body cells, and fertilisation restores the full number.
agreed.evidence: In 1883 Edouard van Beneden studied a roundworm with only 4 chromosomes. He counted 2 in the egg, 2 in the sperm and 4 in the fertilised egg.

agreed.text: Paired chromosomes exchange pieces during meiosis.
agreed.evidence: In 1931 Harriet Creighton and Barbara McClintock used a maize chromosome with a knob that could be seen in a microscope. When the inherited features crossed over, the knob crossed over too.

agreed.text: One blood stem cell can make every kind of blood cell.
agreed.evidence: In 1961 and 1963, James Till, Ernest McCulloch and Andrew Becker showed that each colony of mixed blood cells in a mouse's spleen grew from a single cell.

agreed.text: Some cells die by plan, at fixed times and places, as a normal part of growing.
agreed.evidence: John Sulston followed every cell division in a tiny roundworm. The same 131 cells died in every worm. Robert Horvitz then found genes that the cells need in order to die.

agreed.text: A specialised animal cell still holds the instructions for other jobs.
agreed.evidence: In 2006 Kazutoshi Takahashi and Shinya Yamanaka turned mouse skin cells into stem-like cells by switching on four genes. Laboratories around the world have repeated it.

challenging.claim: A stem cell can become any kind of cell.
challenging.who: A common way of speaking, and many advertisements
challenging.for: It is true of the stem cells in an embryo a few days old. They make every kind of cell in the body.
challenging.against: The stem cells in a child or a grown-up are adult stem cells. A blood stem cell makes blood cells and nothing else. Saying 'any cell' about them is wrong.
challenging.context: This card is about the saying that stem cells can turn into any cell at all.

challenging.claim: When cells die, something has gone wrong in the body.
challenging.for: Cells killed by a burn, a crush or a blocked blood vessel are a real loss, and too much cell death causes some illnesses.
challenging.against: A healthy adult loses many billions of cells every day by plan. Fingers, a working brain and a safe immune system are all made with the help of cells dying on time. Too little cell death is one cause of cancer.
challenging.context: This card is about the idea that the death of a cell is always a failure.

challenging.claim: Stem cell injections can cure almost any illness.
challenging.for: Bone marrow transplants, skin grafts for burns and stem cell repair of the eye's surface are real and well proven.
challenging.against: For most other illnesses there is no good evidence yet. The Indian Council of Medical Research said in its 2017 guidelines that other stem cell treatments may be given only inside proper trials. Unproven injections have harmed people.
challenging.context: This card is about advertisements that offer stem cell treatment for many different illnesses.

challenging.claim: You get exactly one quarter of your DNA from each grandparent.
challenging.who: A simple rule in many books
challenging.for: You get exactly half from each parent, so a quarter from each grandparent is right on average.
challenging.against: Each chromosome your mother gave you is a mix made by crossing over, and each pair was shared out by chance. So one grandmother may have given you 28 parts in 100 and one grandfather 22.
challenging.context: This card is about how much of your DNA comes from each of your four grandparents.

challenging.claim: Meiosis and two parents are a waste. A living being would do better to copy herself.
challenging.who: A real puzzle raised by the biologist John Maynard Smith in the 1970s
challenging.for: A female who copies herself passes on all her instructions, and every one of her young can have young. Some animals do this. Tiny water animals called bdelloid rotifers have been all female for millions of years.
challenging.against: Almost all animals and plants still use meiosis and two parents. The leading idea is that the shuffle keeps a family ahead of fast-changing germs. A study of New Zealand snails found more two-parent breeding in lakes with more parasites.
challenging.context: This card is about why most living beings mix two parents' chromosomes, when simple copying looks easier.

big_questions.q: Your fingers exist because other cells of yours died. Were those cells part of you?
big_questions.hint: They had your DNA and came from the same first cell. Think about what 'part of you' means.

big_questions.q: The same two parents could have had 70 trillion different children. Why are you the one who is here?
big_questions.hint: Think about chance. Is there an answer to 'why this one', or only to 'how'?

big_questions.q: A pudina cell that was part of a stem became a root. A skin cell stays skin. What does 'what I am' mean for a cell?
big_questions.hint: Is a cell's job something she is, or something she is doing?

big_questions.q: A cell that senses damaged DNA takes herself apart. Is that a decision?
big_questions.hint: She senses, compares and acts. Some scientists call it only chemistry. What would make something a decision?

big_questions.q: The egg cell that became you formed inside your mother before she was born. When did you begin?
big_questions.hint: Try several answers: at fertilisation, at that egg, at your grandmother, at the first cell on Earth.

big_questions.q: If doctors could turn your skin cells into any cell, should they be allowed to make egg cells from them?
big_questions.hint: It has been done in mice. Think about who could be helped, and what could go wrong.

big_questions.q: A planarian worm cut in two becomes two worms. Which one is the first worm?
big_questions.hint: Both have the same DNA and both came from the same body. Does the question have an answer?

story.title: Where the Tail Went
story.note: A made-up story. Ammini, Unni and Saramma teacher are imagined. The science is real. A toad tadpole stops eating while the front legs come out, because the mouth and gut are being rebuilt. The cells of the tail die by plan, and cleaner cells carry the material back into the body, where it is used again. Carl Vogt first described planned cell death in 1842, in the tadpoles of a toad. A young toad with new lungs can drown in a steep-sided pot, so anyone who keeps tadpoles gives them a slope to climb out.
text: The rain had come to Wayanad eleven days ago, and it had not stopped for more than an hour since. The ditch behind the pepper vines was full. In the ditch were toad tadpoles, hundreds of them, small and black, like peppercorns with tails.

Ammini was ten. She scooped eleven tadpoles into her grandmother's old bronze uruli, the cracked one that nobody cooked in any more. She set it on the back veranda with ditch water, a stone and a handful of water weed. Every evening she dropped in a boiled leaf of red cheera, and by morning the leaf was lace.

She kept a notebook. On the bottom of a white saucer she had drawn a ruler in ink, with a mark for every millimetre. Each morning she lifted the biggest tadpole into the saucer with a spoonful of water, and read the tail against the marks. The biggest tadpole was called Minnal, which means lightning, because of the way they shot across the uruli when a shadow fell.

For three weeks the tail column in the notebook hardly changed. Thirteen. Fourteen. Fourteen. The back legs came, thin as two threads. Then one morning a front leg pushed out through the skin, elbow first, like an arm through a sleeve. The other followed the next day.
After that the numbers went wrong.
Fourteen became eleven. Eleven became eight. And the cheera leaf lay on the water whole, with not one bite out of it.
"Minnal's tail is falling off," said her brother Unni, who was six. "Like the gecko's did."
Ammini thought so too, and it frightened her. Minnal was not eating. Minnal was getting shorter from the back. She had seen a rotten guava go like that, a little more gone each day.

She did everything she could think of. She changed the water morning and evening. She put in fresh cheera, then a crumb of cooked rice, then a mosquito she had caught herself. She filled the uruli to the brim, so that there would be plenty of clean water. Minnal ate nothing. Minnal sat on the stone and looked at her with eyes that seemed to stand higher on the head than before.
On the fourth morning the tail measured five.

Ammini fetched the torch and her mother's tea strainer. If the tail was falling off, the pieces had to be somewhere. She shone the torch along the bottom of the uruli. Then she poured the water, a cup at a time, through the strainer into a bucket.
She found weed. She found a snail shell, some grit, and the stalk of a cheera leaf. There was no tail, not one black crumb of it. And the water did not smell of anything rotten. It smelled of rain.
She sat down on the veranda step with the notebook on her knees. Unni sat beside her, because he could see that she was thinking and he wanted to be there when it finished.

She wrote down what she knew. The tail was shorter every day. Nothing had been eaten for four days. Nothing was lying on the bottom. Then she looked at Minnal for a long time, and wrote a fourth thing that she had not noticed until now. Minnal was not wasting. The back legs were thicker than last week. The front legs had fingers.
"Legs are made of something," she said slowly. "If Minnal has eaten nothing, what are the legs being made of?"
Unni shrugged.
She read down the tail column. Fourteen, eleven, eight, five. "It isn't falling off," she said. "It's going in."
"In where?"
"Into Minnal. The tail is what Minnal is eating."

She ran through the rain to the next house. Saramma teacher had taught biology at the high school in Kalpetta for thirty years, and now she grew orchids on old coconut husks. She listened to the whole of it without a word. Then she held out her hand for the notebook and read all four lines twice.
"You worked this out from the strainer and the legs?"
Ammini nodded.

"Then you have done what Carl Vogt did in 1842, and he had a microscope. You are right. And it is stranger than you think. Nobody bites the tail. The cells of the tail do it themselves. A signal comes through the blood. Each cell in the tail packs herself into small parcels. Cleaner cells swallow the parcels and carry the material back into the body. Part of each new leg was once tail."
"The cells die on purpose?"
"They die on time. Hold up your hand."
Ammini held it up.
"Spread your fingers. Before you were born, that hand was a little paddle with no gaps in it. The cells between your fingers did what Minnal's tail is doing now. That is why you can hold a pen."
Ammini looked at the gaps between her fingers. Through each gap she could see the rain falling on the pepper vines.
"Now," said Saramma teacher. "How deep is the water in your uruli?"
"To the top. I kept filling it. I wanted them to have plenty."
"A toad with new lungs and no tail does not want plenty of water. They want a way out of it."

Ammini ran home faster than she had come. She tipped out half the water. She found a broken roof tile behind the woodshed and leaned it from the bottom of the uruli to the rim, like a road. Unni held it steady while she packed the stone under it.
By evening Minnal sat on the tile, halfway up. The tail was a stub of two millimetres. Minnal's throat went in and out, in and out, breathing air.
Ammini opened the notebook. Under fourteen, eleven, eight, five and two, she wrote a nought. Then she crossed the nought out. Beside it she wrote: all of it, inside.
In the morning the tile was empty. Out by the pepper vines, something the size of her thumbnail hopped once, and was gone into the wet grass.
story.epiphany: For the parent: nothing fell off, and nothing was lost. A tadpole's tail is taken apart by the tail's own cells, which die by plan when a signal arrives in the blood, and the material is reused to finish the legs. Ammini's mistake was to treat a planned ending as an illness and try to stop it. Your child's own fingers were freed in the same way before birth.
ask: Ammini found no pieces of tail in the strainer. What did that tell her?
Minnal ate nothing for four days, yet the legs grew thicker. Where did the material come from?
How is a tail that is taken apart by plan different from a guava that rots?
Which parts of your own body were shaped by cells dying on time?
Why did Ammini lower the water and add a slope at the end?
