games.title: Divide, Wait, Change or Die?
games.context: This is a card game about the choices a cell has. Each card describes one cell at one moment. You decide what that cell does next: divide by mitosis, divide by meiosis, specialise (take on one special job), wait, or die by plan. The answer and the reason are on the back.

printables.title: 24 cell cards to cut out (the answer is on the back)

items.f: A skin cell at the edge of a fresh scrape on a knee.
items.b: DIVIDE BY MITOSIS. The gap must be filled with more skin cells of the same kind.

items.f: A cell inside the anther of a hibiscus flower, where pollen is made.
items.b: DIVIDE BY MEIOSIS. Pollen leads to sperm cells, which need half the chromosomes.

items.f: A cell between two fingers in the hand of a human embryo seven weeks old.
items.b: DIE BY PLAN. The cells between the fingers die, and that separates the fingers.

items.f: A skin cell whose DNA was badly damaged by strong sun and cannot be repaired.
items.b: DIE BY PLAN. A cell with broken instructions could start a cancer, so she takes herself apart.

items.f: A blood stem cell in bone marrow. The body needs more red blood cells.
items.b: DIVIDE BY MITOSIS. One daughter stays a stem cell. The other goes on to become a blood cell.

items.f: A new daughter of a blood stem cell. A signal says: carry oxygen.
items.b: SPECIALISE. She fills up with the red protein that holds oxygen and becomes a red blood cell.

items.f: A cell in a testis, at the last stage before sperm cells are made.
items.b: DIVIDE BY MEIOSIS. One cell becomes four sperm cells with 23 chromosomes each.

items.f: A cell in the tail of a tadpole whose front legs have just come out.
items.b: DIE BY PLAN. A signal in the blood tells the tail cells to take themselves apart. The material is reused.

items.f: A skin cell in the middle of healthy skin, touching neighbours on every side.
items.b: WAIT. There is no gap to fill. She stays as she is and carries on working.

items.f: A cell at the very tip of a moong sprout's root.
items.b: DIVIDE BY MITOSIS. Root tips are growing points, where cells keep dividing.

items.f: A young nerve cell in a growing brain. She has not linked up with any other cell.
items.b: DIE BY PLAN. A growing brain makes extra nerve cells and keeps the ones that link up well.

items.f: A cell taken over by a virus. A defender cell gives her the death signal.
items.b: DIE BY PLAN. When she dies neatly, the virus inside her cannot go on multiplying.

items.f: A cell beside the node of a pudina cutting that has stood in water for three days.
items.b: DIVIDE BY MITOSIS. She goes back to dividing, and her daughters build a new root.

items.f: A fertilised human egg, one day old.
items.b: DIVIDE BY MITOSIS. One cell becomes two, then four, then eight, each with all 46 chromosomes.

items.f: A cell on the outside of a very young embryo. Her neighbours signal: you are at the surface.
items.b: SPECIALISE. Cells take their jobs from signals around them. She starts on the path to skin.

items.f: An egg cell in the ovary of a girl of ten.
items.b: WAIT. She began meiosis before the girl was born and has been paused ever since.

items.f: A liver cell, just after a surgeon has removed part of the liver.
items.b: DIVIDE BY MITOSIS. Liver cells start dividing again until the liver is back to full size.

items.f: A cell in a young stem. She has built a thick wall and is to become part of a water pipe.
items.b: DIE BY PLAN. She dies and empties herself. Her hollow wall stays as a pipe for water.

items.f: A young defender cell in training. Tests show that she would attack the body's own cells.
items.b: DIE BY PLAN. Defender cells that would attack the body are removed during training. This keeps the body safe.

items.f: A dividing cell. Every chromosome but one is held by threads from both sides.
items.b: WAIT. This is a checkpoint. She pulls the copies apart only when every chromosome is held.

items.f: A yeast cell in warm bun dough with plenty of sugar.
items.b: DIVIDE BY MITOSIS. With food and warmth, yeast cells copy themselves about every two hours.

items.f: A cell of the gut lining, four days old, at the tip of a tiny finger of the gut wall.
items.b: DIE BY PLAN. Her work is done. She lets go and dies, and a newer cell takes her place.

items.f: A muscle cell in the heart of a grown woman.
items.b: WAIT. Heart muscle cells almost never divide. Most of them work for a whole lifetime.

items.f: A cell under a fern leaf, inside one of the small brown dots where spores are made.
items.b: DIVIDE BY MEIOSIS. Fern spores have half the chromosomes, so they are made by meiosis.

printables.title: 5 answer cards for each player (make one set each)

rules: Shuffle the 24 cell cards and put them in a pile, with the cell side up. Each player holds a set of 5 answer cards.
One player reads the top card aloud.
Count to three together. Everyone lays one answer card face down, then all turn them over.
Turn the cell card over and read the answer and the reason. Each player with the right answer gets 1 point.
If nobody is right, put the cell card back in the middle of the pile.
The game ends when the pile is gone. The player with the most points wins. Playing alone, 18 points or more is a win.

setup.art: A pile of cell cards on a floor mat, and two players each holding a fan of five answer cards.
setup.caption: 1. Put the cell cards in a pile. Each player takes five answer cards.

setup.art: A child reading a card aloud while another player lays an answer card face down.
setup.caption: 2. Read the card. Count to three. Lay down your answer.

setup.art: A cell card turned over to show its answer, with one player's matching answer card beside it.
setup.caption: 3. Turn the cell card over. A right answer wins a point.

flow.do: 1. Cut out the 24 cell cards. 2. Write the five answers on slips of paper, one set for each player. 3. Shuffle the cell cards.
flow.say: Each card describes one cell at one moment. A cell has five choices: divide by mitosis, divide by meiosis, specialise, wait, or die by plan. Let's read the five answer slips first.
flow.kid: Cut out the cards. Make five answer slips. Shuffle the cell cards.
flow.parent: Read the five answers aloud once. 'Wait' means the cell stays as she is and carries on with her work.
flow.context: This is the first step of Divide, Wait, Change or Die? Here you make the cards and learn the five answers.

flow.do: 1. Read the top card aloud. 2. Count to three. 3. Everyone lays down an answer. 4. Turn the card over and read the reason.
flow.say: Ask two questions each time. Does the body need more cells here? Would this cell be a danger if she stayed?
flow.kid: Read the card. Lay down your answer. Then read the back.

ask.q: Why does a pollen-making cell in a flower use meiosis, but a root tip cell uses mitosis?
good: The anther makes pollen, which leads to sex cells, and they need half the chromosomes.
A root only needs more cells of the same kind.

flow.parent: Children often choose 'divide' for every card. If that happens, ask what would go wrong if this cell made more of herself.
flow.context: This is the main part of Divide, Wait, Change or Die? Here you read each cell card and choose what the cell does.

flow.do: 1. Count the points. 2. Sort all 24 cards into five heaps by their answers. 3. Count the cards in each heap.
flow.say: Which heap is the biggest? Which answer surprised you most? Let's look at the 'die by plan' heap together.
flow.kid: Count your points. Sort the cards into five heaps. Which heap is biggest?

check.q: A skin cell has DNA damage that cannot be repaired. What is the safest thing for the body?
options: She divides quickly to replace herself
She dies by plan
She turns into a stem cell
check.why: A cell with broken instructions could pass the damage to her daughters and start a cancer. So she takes herself apart. Choosing 'divides quickly' usually comes from thinking that more cells are always good. Here dividing would spread the damage.

flow.parent: The 'die by plan' heap has eight cards and the mitosis heap has seven. Ask your child to look at the eight together. Each one is shaping, choosing or safety.
flow.context: This is the last step of Divide, Wait, Change or Die? Here you count the points and sort the cards by answer.

experiments.title: The Pudina Pieces Test: which piece of a stem can grow roots?
experiments.context: In this experiment you cut pudina (mint) stems into four kinds of pieces and stand them in water for nine days. Some pieces have a node, which is the place where leaves join the stem. Some have none. You find out which pieces can grow new roots.
experiments.question: Which part of a pudina stem can grow new roots: a piece with a node, a piece from between two nodes, or a leaf alone? And does a piece need its leaves to do it?
experiments.predict: Guess first. Which of the four kinds of pieces will grow roots, and which will not? Say why you think so. Then guess where on a piece the roots will come out: from the cut end, or from somewhere else. Write your guesses down.
experiments.fair_test: Cut all the pieces from the same bunch on the same day. Give every kind the same water and the same bright window, out of hot sun. Change the water for all of them every two days. Use five pieces of each kind, because one piece alone can fail by bad luck.

materials.item: a fresh bunch of pudina (mint) with at least 5 firm stems, each 12 centimetres or longer
small scissors
a glass tumbler
steel katoris or saucers
paper slips and a pencil for labels
a ruler
a magnifying glass, if you have one

experiments.safety: A grown-up cuts the stems, or watches closely while the child cuts with small scissors.

schedule.what: Cut five pieces of each of the four kinds. Stand them in water. Write down your guesses.
Change the water. Count the pieces with roots or white bumps.
Change the water. Count the pieces with roots. Note where the roots come out.
Change the water. Count again and measure the longest root.
Make the last count. Fill in the table and explain the result.

experiments.record: Fill in the table on days 3, 5, 7 and 9. Draw one piece of each kind on day 9 and mark where the roots are, or take a photo of each. Then write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why you think it happened.

example_chart.title: Made-up example results: pieces with roots, out of 5
example_chart.note: These numbers are made up, to show what a finished table can look like. Your numbers will be different.

setup.art: A pudina stem lying on a table with dotted cut lines marking four pieces: a top piece with two nodes and leaves, a short piece with one bare node, a short bare piece from between two nodes, and one single leaf.
setup.caption: 1. From each stem cut four pieces: A with a node and leaves, B with a bare node, C from between two nodes, D a leaf alone.

setup.art: A glass tumbler holding five leafy pudina pieces with their lower nodes under water, beside three steel katoris of shallow water labelled B, C and D with small pieces lying in them.
setup.caption: 2. Stand the A pieces in a tumbler. Lay the B, C and D pieces in shallow water in three katoris.

setup.art: A child looking through a magnifying glass at a pudina piece with thin white roots growing out at a node.
setup.caption: 3. Every two days, change the water and count the pieces with roots.

flow.do: 1. Look at one pudina stem together. 2. Find the nodes, the small bumps where each pair of leaves joins. 3. Find the bare lengths of stem between the nodes.
flow.say: Run a finger down the stem. Where do the leaves join? Those places are called nodes. What is between them?
flow.kid: Run a finger down the stem. Find where the leaves join. Those are nodes.
flow.parent: Pudina leaves grow in pairs. The gaps between nodes are longest near the bottom of the stem. Choose firm green stems and leave any black or limp ones.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Pudina Pieces Test. Here you find the nodes on a pudina stem.

flow.do: 1. Describe the four kinds of pieces. 2. Ask which kinds will grow roots, and why. 3. Ask where on a piece the roots will come out. 4. Write the guesses down.
flow.say: Which of these four pieces will grow roots? Why do you think so? And where will the roots come out?
flow.kid: Guess which pieces will grow roots. Say why. Guess where the roots will come out. Write it down.

good: Any reason is fine at this stage.
The piece with leaves can make food, so it may grow best.
Roots may come from the cut end, because that is where the stem is open.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Many children expect roots from the cut end, and expect every piece of stem to root.
flow.context: This step of the Pudina Pieces Test is for guessing. You guess before you cut any stem.

flow.do: 1. From the top of a stem, cut piece A: about 6 centimetres, with two nodes. Pull the leaves off the lower node only. 2. Lower down, cut piece B: one node in the middle of about 3 centimetres of stem. Pull off its leaves. 3. Cut piece C from between two nodes, with no node on it. 4. Pick one large leaf with its stalk as piece D. 5. Do the same with four more stems.
flow.say: From every stem we cut the same four pieces. A has a node and leaves. B has a node and no leaves. C has no node. D is a leaf alone.
flow.kid: Cut four pieces from each stem. A has a node and leaves. B has a bare node. C has no node. D is one leaf.
flow.parent: Piece C will be short, perhaps 2 centimetres. That is fine. Look at both ends of C to be sure there is no node on it. Cut with a clean snip and do not crush the stem.
flow.context: This step of the Pudina Pieces Test is the cutting. Here you cut five pieces of each of the four kinds.

flow.do: 1. Stand the five A pieces in a tumbler, with the lower node under 3 centimetres of water. 2. Lay the B, C and D pieces in three katoris, in water 1 centimetre deep. 3. Label each one. 4. Put them all at a bright window, out of hot sun.
flow.say: All four kinds get the same water and the same light. That keeps the test fair.
flow.kid: Stand the A pieces in the tumbler. Lay B, C and D in shallow water. Label them. Put them by a bright window.

ask.q: Why five pieces of each kind?
good: One piece could fail by bad luck.
If four or five of a kind do the same thing, we can trust the result more.

flow.wait: Leave them for 2 days, then change the water
flow.context: This step of the Pudina Pieces Test puts the pieces in water at a bright window.

flow.do: 1. On days 3, 5 and 7, pour off the old water and add fresh water. 2. Look at every piece, with a magnifying glass if you have one. 3. Count the pieces that have white bumps or roots. 4. Write down where on the piece the roots are. 5. On day 7, measure the longest root.
flow.say: Look for small white bumps first. They are roots just starting. On which kinds do you see them? Where on the piece are they?
flow.kid: Change the water. Look for white bumps and roots. Count them. Where on the piece are they?
flow.parent: The first white bumps often show by day 3 or 4, at the node. In cool weather everything takes a few days longer, so carry on to day 12. Throw out any piece that turns black and slimy, and write that down as a result.
flow.context: This step of the Pudina Pieces Test is the checking. Every two days you change the water and count the pieces with roots.

flow.do: 1. On day 9, count one last time and fill in the table. 2. Ask your child for the three sentences. 3. Ask which two kinds of pieces show whether leaves are needed. 4. Ask your child to point to where on the piece the root-making cells must be. 5. Only then read the explanation together.
flow.say: Say what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why. Now compare B and D. One has a node and no leaf. The other has a leaf and no node.
flow.kid: Say what you guessed. Say what you saw. Say why. Point to where the root-making cells are.

ask.q: Piece B had no leaves and piece D was only a leaf. What do those two tell us?
good: B grew roots without leaves, so leaves are not what makes roots.
D had a leaf and no node and grew no roots, so the node is what matters.

ask.q: The roots came out at the node, not at the cut end. What does that tell us about the cells there?
good: Cells that can start dividing again are at the node.
The rest of the stem is finished and does not make new parts.

flow.parent: The usual result is that A and B grow roots at the node, and C and D do not. B is often slower than A, because leaves supply food. If a C piece does grow a root, look again for a node hidden at one end. Plant the rooted A pieces in a pot of soil, and they will grow into pudina plants.

check.q: In the Pudina Pieces Test, a bare piece of stem with a node grew roots. A leaf alone did not. What does this show?
options: Roots need leaves to make food for them
Cells that can make new roots are at the node
Every part of a stem can make roots
check.why: The bare node had no leaves and still grew roots. The leaf had no node and grew none. So the cells that can start dividing again are at the node. Choosing 'leaves' is a sensible first idea, because leaves make food. But the bare node shows that stored food was enough to start.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Pudina Pieces Test. Here you make the last count and explain the result.

experiments.title: The Shuffle Test: how many different egg cells can one mother make?
experiments.context: In this experiment three coins stand for three pairs of chromosomes in a mother's cell. One toss of all three coins makes one egg cell. You make 24 egg cells and count how many different kinds you get.
experiments.question: If a cell has three pairs of chromosomes, how many different egg cells can meiosis make? What happens to that number when there are four pairs?
experiments.predict: Guess first. In 24 tosses of three coins, how many different results will you get? Will any result come up more than once? Say why you think so, and write your guesses down.
experiments.fair_test: Toss all the coins together each time, from the same tumbler, onto the same cloth. Write down every toss, even the ones that repeat. Do not skip a toss because it looks boring.

materials.item: three different coins, such as 1 rupee, 2 rupees and 5 rupees
a fourth coin of another kind, such as 10 rupees
a steel tumbler to shake the coins in
a folded towel to toss onto
paper and a pencil

schedule.what: Toss three coins 24 times and count the different results. List every possible result. Then work out the number for four coins and for 23 pairs.

experiments.record: Fill in the table for all 24 tosses. Then write the list of every possible result for three coins. Write three sentences: what you thought would happen, what you saw, and why.

example_chart.title: Made-up example: the first six egg cells (M is the mother's mother's chromosome, F is the mother's father's)
example_chart.note: These tosses are made up, to show how to fill in the table. Your tosses will be different.

setup.art: Three different coins in a row on a table, each with a small label: pair 1, pair 2, pair 3, and a note that heads means M and tails means F.
setup.caption: 1. Each coin is one pair of chromosomes. Heads is M, the chromosome from the mother's mother. Tails is F, from the mother's father.

setup.art: A child tipping three coins out of a steel tumbler onto a folded towel.
setup.caption: 2. Shake the three coins in a tumbler and tip them out. That is one egg cell.

setup.art: A notebook page with a table of tosses written as rows of M and F, and a tick beside each new result.
setup.caption: 3. Write down each egg cell. Tick the ones you have not seen before.

flow.do: 1. Lay the three coins in a row and call them pair 1, pair 2 and pair 3. 2. Explain that heads is M and tails is F. 3. Draw the table with 24 rows.
flow.say: A mother has two of each chromosome, one from her mother and one from her father. An egg gets only one of each pair. The coin decides which. Heads, M, is the chromosome she got from her own mother. Tails, F, is the one from her own father.
flow.kid: Lay out three coins. Each coin is one pair. Heads is M. Tails is F. Draw a table with 24 rows.
flow.parent: M stands for the chromosome this mother got from her own mother. F is the one she got from her father. Always read the coins in the same order: 1 rupee, 2 rupees, 5 rupees.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Shuffle Test. Here you set up three coins to stand for three pairs of chromosomes.

flow.do: 1. Ask how many different results 24 tosses will give, and why. 2. Ask whether any result will repeat, and why. 3. Write the guesses down.
flow.say: We will make 24 egg cells. How many different kinds will there be? Will any kind come up twice? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how many different results you will get. Will any repeat? Say why. Write it down.

good: Any reason is fine at this stage.
There are only a few ways three coins can fall, so some must repeat.

flow.parent: Do not correct the guesses. Some children expect 24 different results, and some expect only 3 or 6.
flow.context: This step of the Shuffle Test is for guessing. You guess before you toss any coin.

flow.do: 1. Shake the three coins in the tumbler and tip them onto the towel. 2. Write M or F for each coin, in order. 3. Write 'yes' if this result has come up before. 4. Do this 24 times.
flow.say: Each toss is one egg cell. Read the coins in order and I will write them down. Have we seen this one before?
flow.kid: Shake the coins and tip them out. Write M or F for each coin. Have you seen this one before? Do it 24 times.
flow.parent: Take turns to toss and to write. Most families see 7 or 8 different results in 24 tosses, and never more than 8.
flow.context: This step of the Shuffle Test is the tossing. Each toss of three coins makes one egg cell.

flow.do: 1. Count the different results. 2. Ask your child to list every possible result, in a careful order, to see if any is missing. 3. Start with one coin, then two coins, then three.
flow.say: How many different eggs did we get? Could there be one we never tossed? Let's list them all. Start with just one coin.
flow.kid: Count the different results. Now list every possible one. Start with one coin. Then two. Then three.

ask.q: One coin gives 2 results and two coins give 4. Why do three coins give 8?
good: Each of the 4 results can have M or F added for the third coin.
Every extra coin doubles the number.

flow.parent: A careful list is MMM, MMF, MFM, MFF, FMM, FMF, FFM, FFF. Let your child find the order. The idea to reach is that each extra pair doubles the number.
flow.context: This step of the Shuffle Test is for counting. You list every possible egg cell for three pairs of chromosomes.

flow.do: 1. Add the fourth coin. Ask how many results are possible now, and why. 2. Toss the four coins 10 times to see some of them. 3. Carry the doubling on in a table up to 10 pairs. 4. Read out the number for 23 pairs: 8,388,608. 5. Ask for the three sentences.
flow.say: Four pairs now. How many different eggs? A human has 23 pairs. Keep doubling and see how far you get.
flow.kid: Add a fourth coin. How many results now? Keep doubling up to 10 pairs. Then hear the number for 23 pairs.

ask.q: Two children of the same mother and father are never copies, unless they are identical twins. Why?
good: Each egg gets a different mix of the mother's chromosomes.
Each sperm gets a different mix too, and there are millions of possible mixes.

flow.parent: The doubling goes 2, 4, 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, 256, 512, 1,024 for ten pairs. Real meiosis mixes even more than the coins do, because paired chromosomes also swap pieces.

check.q: In the Shuffle Test, each extra pair of chromosomes changed the number of possible egg cells. How?
options: It added 2 more
It doubled the number
It did not change the number
check.why: Every result so far can be followed by M or by F for the new pair, so the number doubles. Three pairs give 8, four give 16, and 23 give 8,388,608. Choosing 'added 2' fits the step from one pair to two, but it does not fit the step from two pairs to three.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Shuffle Test. Here you add a fourth pair and carry the pattern on to a human's 23 pairs.

activities.title: Paddle to Hand: how do you get fingers out of a paddle?
activities.context: In this activity you make a small hand out of dough in two ways. One way adds fingers on. The other way starts with a flat paddle and takes dough away. Then you find out which way your own hand was made before you were born.

materials.item: two balls of atta dough or clay, each the size of a lemon
an ice cream stick or a blunt butter knife
a steel plate to work on

activities.record: Take a photo of both dough hands. Say which parts of the paddle had to go. Or draw the paddle and shade those parts.

setup.art: A child pressing five small rolls of dough onto a round dough palm on a steel plate.
setup.caption: 1. Hand one: roll five fingers and stick them onto a palm.

setup.art: A flat paddle of dough with four thin wedges being cut out of it with an ice cream stick.
setup.caption: 2. Hand two: flatten a paddle and cut four wedges out of it.

setup.art: A child's real hand with the fingers spread wide, and a small arrow pointing to the little web of skin at the base of two fingers.
setup.caption: 3. Spread your own fingers and find the small web left at the bottom.

flow.do: 1. Give your child both balls of dough. 2. With the first, roll a palm and five fingers and stick the fingers on. 3. With the second, flatten a paddle shaped like a mitten. 4. Cut four thin wedges out of the paddle to leave five fingers.
flow.say: Make one hand by adding fingers. Make the other by starting with a paddle and taking dough away.
flow.kid: Make one hand by sticking fingers on. Make the other by cutting wedges out of a paddle.
flow.parent: The stuck-on fingers often fall off, and the cut hand holds together. Let your child notice that without being told.
flow.context: This is the first step of Paddle to Hand. Here you make a dough hand in two ways.

flow.do: 1. Ask which way a real hand is made before birth, and why. 2. Wait for the guess and the reason. 3. Ask what would have to happen to the cells in the wedges.
flow.say: Before you were born, your hand had to be made. Which way do you think your body did it? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Guess how your real hand was made. By adding, or by taking away? Say why.

ask.q: If the body started with a paddle, what must happen to the cells between the fingers?
good: They have to go.
They have to die and be cleared away.

flow.parent: Most children say 'adding', because growing seems to mean adding. Do not correct it yet.
flow.context: This step of Paddle to Hand is for guessing. You guess how a real hand is made before birth.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child that a hand begins as a flat paddle, when the embryo is about five weeks old. 2. Finger bones form inside the paddle, and the cells between them die by plan. 3. Have your child spread their fingers and find the small web at the base. 4. Tell them a duck's foot keeps its web.
flow.say: Your hand began as a paddle. Finger bones formed inside. Then the cells in between died on time. Spread your fingers. Can you find a little web left over?
flow.kid: Your hand began as a paddle. The cells between the fingers died on time. Spread your fingers. Find the little web.
flow.parent: The full picture uses both ways. The fingers do grow longer, and the cells between them die. In a duck embryo the cells between the toes get a signal that blocks the dying, so the web stays.

check.q: Before birth, a hand is a flat paddle. How do the fingers become separate?
options: The fingers grow out and nothing dies
The cells between the fingers die by plan
The paddle tears along weak lines
check.why: The cells between the finger bones die by plan and are cleared away. Choosing 'grow out' is half right, because the fingers do lengthen. But without the planned death the fingers would stay joined, like a duck's toes.

flow.context: This is the last step of Paddle to Hand. Here you learn how real fingers are separated and look at your own hand.

activities.title: Double Trouble: what happens if nobody halves the chromosomes?
activities.context: In this activity seeds stand for the chromosomes of a pea plant, who has 14. You pass them on from parents to children with no halving and watch the number grow. Then you work out what the plant must do, and find that not just any half will do.

materials.item: rajma, chana or any large seeds
steel katoris
14 slips of paper
two sketch pens, red and blue

activities.record: Write the number of seeds in each generation. Then write one sentence: what must a pea plant do before making a pea egg cell or sperm cell, and why?

setup.art: Two steel katoris each holding 14 rajma seeds, with both being tipped into one bigger katori below them.
setup.caption: 1. Each parent has 14. Tip both into the child's katori and count.

setup.art: Fourteen paper slips on a table numbered 1 to 7 in red and 1 to 7 in blue, with a hand picking seven of them without looking.
setup.caption: 2. Number the slips 1 to 7 in red and 1 to 7 in blue. Pick any seven without looking.

flow.do: 1. Count 14 seeds into each of two katoris. These are two pea plant parents. 2. Tip both into a third katori, for the child, and count. 3. Make a second child katori with the same number. 4. Tip two children together for a grandchild, and count.
flow.say: A pea plant has 14 chromosomes. Suppose each parent gives all 14. How many does the child have? And the grandchild?
flow.kid: Put 14 seeds in two katoris. Tip both into one. Count. Do it again for a grandchild.

ask.q: What is happening to the number in each generation?
good: It doubles: 14, 28, 56.
It would be 112 next, and then 224.

flow.context: This is the first step of Double Trouble. Here seeds stand for chromosomes, and nothing is halved.

flow.do: 1. Tell your child that pea plants have had 14 chromosomes for a very long time. 2. Ask what the plant must do to keep the number at 14. 3. Wait for the idea and the reason.
flow.say: Real pea plants always have 14. The number never doubles. So what must a plant do before passing chromosomes on? Why?
flow.kid: Real pea plants always have 14. So what must the plant do first? Say why.

good: Half: 7 from each parent.
7 and 7 make 14 again.

flow.parent: Let your child reach 'half' without help. Then ask the next question: which half?
flow.context: This step of Double Trouble asks how a pea plant keeps the same number of chromosomes in every generation.

flow.do: 1. Number seven slips 1 to 7 in red and seven slips 1 to 7 in blue. Red came from the plant's mother and blue from the father. 2. Mix the 14 slips face down. 3. Your child picks any 7 without looking. 4. Turn them over and check which numbers are there.
flow.say: Each number is one kind of chromosome. Pick any seven. Now look. Do you have one of every number?
flow.kid: Mix the slips face down. Pick any seven. Turn them over. Do you have every number from 1 to 7?

ask.q: Your seven slips are missing a number and have another one twice. Why is that a problem?
good: The new plant would have no instructions of that kind from this parent.
It would have too many of another kind.

flow.parent: A random seven almost never has one of each number. The chance is about 1 in 27. If your child is lucky the first time, pick again.
flow.context: This step of Double Trouble tests whether any half of the chromosomes will do.

flow.do: 1. Ask your child to invent a way of sharing that always gives one of each number. 2. Try it: lay the slips in pairs, 1 with 1 and 2 with 2, then send one of each pair each way. 3. Say that this pairing up is what a cell does in meiosis.
flow.say: Can you find a way to share them so that each side always gets one of every number? Try it, and show me.
flow.kid: Invent a way to share the slips. Test it, and show your grown-up.
flow.parent: The answer is to pair the slips first and then separate each pair. Whether red or blue goes left is free, and that freedom is the shuffle.

check.q: A pea plant has 14 chromosomes, in 7 matching pairs. Which chromosomes does a pea egg cell get?
options: Any 7 of the 14
One from each of the 7 pairs
All 14
check.why: The egg cell needs one of each kind, so she gets one chromosome from each pair. 'Any 7' gives the right number but could leave a kind out. 'All 14' would double the number in every generation.

flow.context: This is the last step of Double Trouble. Here you design a way to halve the chromosomes without losing any kind.

activities.title: Two Dances: mitosis and meiosis with paper chromosomes
activities.context: In this activity paper strips stand for the chromosomes of a cell with two matching pairs. You take the same cell through mitosis and then through meiosis, and compare the cells you end up with.

materials.item: paper strips: 4 long and 4 short
red and blue sketch pens
paper clips
a piece of string about 1 metre long, for the edge of the cell
scissors and sticky tape

activities.safety: Take care with the scissors when you cut the strips.
activities.record: Take a photo of the two cells that mitosis made and the four that meiosis made, or draw them. Next to each cell, write how many chromosomes are in it.

setup.art: A loop of string on a table with four paper strips inside it: a long red, a long blue, a short red and a short blue.
setup.caption: 1. The cell has two pairs: a long pair and a short pair. Red came from the mother and blue from the father.

setup.art: Each strip clipped to an identical copy to make four X shapes, lined up in single file across the middle of the string loop.
setup.caption: 2. Mitosis: copy each strip, line the four X shapes up one by one, and unclip.

setup.art: The four X shapes lined up as two side-by-side pairs across the middle of the string loop, with the tips of the long red and long blue strips swapped.
setup.caption: 3. Meiosis: copy each strip, line the X shapes up as partners, swap tips, and divide twice.

flow.do: 1. Colour one long and one short strip red, and one long and one short strip blue. 2. Lay the string in a loop and put these four strips inside. 3. Make a copy of each strip with the spare strips, and clip each copy to its original to make an X.
flow.say: This cell has four chromosomes, in two pairs. Before any division, the cell copies every chromosome. The copies stay clipped together.
flow.kid: Colour the strips. Put four inside the string. Copy each one. Clip each copy to its strip.
flow.parent: The two long strips are a matching pair, and so are the two short ones. A clipped X is one chromosome with its copy, not two different chromosomes.
flow.context: This is the first step of Two Dances. Here you make a paper cell with two pairs of chromosomes and copy them.

flow.do: 1. Line the four X shapes up one below another across the middle of the loop. 2. Unclip each X and slide one strip to the left and its copy to the right. 3. Pinch the string loop into two loops. 4. Count and name the strips in each new cell.
flow.say: This is mitosis. One copy of every chromosome goes each way. Count the strips in each new cell.
flow.kid: Line up the four X shapes. Unclip them. Send one copy each way. Count the strips in each new cell.

ask.q: How do the two new cells compare with the cell you started with?
good: Each has the same four chromosomes: long red, long blue, short red, short blue.
They are copies of the first cell.

flow.context: This step of Two Dances is mitosis. One cell becomes two cells with the same chromosomes.

flow.do: 1. Put the strips back as four clipped X shapes in one loop. 2. This time lay the long red X beside the long blue X, and the short red beside the short blue. 3. Cut the tip off one long red strip and one long blue strip, swap the tips and tape them on. 4. First division: send one whole X of each pair to each side, and pinch the loop in two. 5. Second division: unclip each X and send one strip each way.
flow.say: This is meiosis. Partners line up side by side and swap a piece. The first division parts the partners. The second parts the copies.
flow.kid: Lay partners side by side. Swap two tips. First send whole X shapes apart. Then unclip and divide again.
flow.parent: At the first division, toss a coin for each pair to decide whether red goes left or right. That is the chance sharing from the Shuffle Test. You should end with four small loops, each holding one long strip and one short strip.
flow.context: This step of Two Dances is meiosis. One cell divides twice and becomes four cells with half the chromosomes.

flow.do: 1. Lay the two mitosis cells and the four meiosis cells side by side. 2. Count the strips in each. 3. Ask your child what is the same and what is different. 4. Take a photo of both results.
flow.say: Look at both results. How many cells? How many chromosomes in each?
flow.kid: Put both results side by side. Count the cells. Count the strips in each.

ask.q: Why are the four meiosis cells not all the same?
good: The swapped tips made a strip that is part red and part blue.
Each cell got a different mix of red and blue.

check.q: A cell with 4 chromosomes divides by meiosis. What does she make?
options: 2 cells with 4 chromosomes each
4 cells with 2 chromosomes each
4 cells with 4 chromosomes each
check.why: Meiosis copies the chromosomes once and divides twice, so there are four cells with half the number. '2 cells with 4 each' is what mitosis makes. '4 cells with 4 each' would need the chromosomes to be copied twice.

flow.context: This is the last step of Two Dances. Here you compare the cells made by mitosis and by meiosis.

activities.title: The Dead on Purpose Hunt: find cells that finished their work by dying
activities.context: In this activity you search your home and your own body for things made of cells that died by plan. The dead cells are not waste. Their dying is what made them useful.

materials.item: paper and a pencil
a magnifying glass, if you have one

activities.record: Make a list with three columns: the thing, the living being it came from, and the job the dead cells do.

setup.art: A child looking at the tip of a fingernail and a strand of hair through a magnifying glass.
setup.caption: 1. Start with your own body: nails, hair and the top layer of skin.

setup.art: A wooden rolling board, a coir rope, a cotton towel and a dried ridge gourd scrubber laid out on a kitchen floor.
setup.caption: 2. Then search the home: wood, coir, cotton and a dried gourd scrubber.

flow.do: 1. Ask whether any part of your child's body is made of dead cells, and how they could tell. 2. Wait for ideas. 3. Test them: which parts can be cut with no pain and no bleeding?
flow.say: Is any part of your body made of dead cells? How could you tell? Which parts can be cut without any pain?
flow.kid: Which parts of your body can be cut with no pain? Point to them.

ask.q: Why does cutting a nail or a hair not hurt?
good: The cells there are already dead.
They filled up with a tough protein, and then died by plan.

flow.parent: Hair, nails and the top layer of skin are cells that filled with a tough protein called keratin and then died by plan. The living part is at the root.
flow.context: This is the first step of the Dead on Purpose Hunt. Here you find the dead cells on your own body.

flow.do: 1. Walk round the home and find things that came from plants or other animals. 2. Look for wood, coir, cotton, jute, a dried gourd scrubber, a feather, wool. 3. For each one, ask what job the dead cells did in the living being.
flow.say: Wood was once part of a living tree. What job did these cells do in the tree? Did they do it alive or dead?
flow.kid: Find wood, coir, cotton or a feather. What job did those cells do? Write each one down.
flow.parent: In a tree, the cells that carry water die by plan and become hollow pipes. Wood is mostly these pipes and stiff dead fibres. A dried ridge gourd scrubber is the gourd's net of water pipes. Feathers and wool are like hair.
flow.context: This step of the Dead on Purpose Hunt searches the home for things made of cells that died by plan.

flow.do: 1. Count the items on the list. 2. Ask what the tree would lose if the pipe cells refused to die. 3. Ask your child to finish the sentence: 'These cells were useful because…'
flow.say: A tree's water pipes work only because the cells inside died and emptied. What would happen if they stayed alive and full?
flow.kid: Count your list. Finish the sentence: 'These cells were useful because…'

check.q: A tree's water-carrying cells die when they are fully built. Why does that help the tree?
options: Dead cells need no food
The empty cells become open pipes for water
The tree has too many cells
check.why: A living cell is full, so water could not flow through her quickly. When she dies and empties, her stiff wall is left as a pipe. 'Dead cells need no food' is true, but it is not the reason. The reason is the open pipe.

flow.context: This is the last step of the Dead on Purpose Hunt. Here you think about why the dying was useful.

projects.title: Kitchen Regrowers: where does a vegetable keep the cells that can still divide?
projects.context: In this ten-day project you put pieces of kitchen vegetables in water and see which pieces can grow again. Then you find the exact place on each piece where the new growth starts.

materials.item: an onion
a carrot with the top still on
a potato with small 'eyes' on the skin
garlic cloves
saucers or shallow katoris
a knife, for the grown-up
a magnifying glass, if you have one

projects.safety: A grown-up does all the cutting with the knife.

schedule.what: Cut the pieces, guess which will regrow, and stand them in shallow water.
Change the water. Look for the first new growth and mark where it starts.
Change the water. Measure the new shoots and roots.
Make the last drawing of each piece and explain where the growing cells were.

projects.record: Take a photo of each piece on day 1 and on day 10, or draw it. Mark the place where new growth started. Write one sentence for each piece: did it regrow, and from where?

setup.art: Six saucers in a row holding an onion base, an onion middle slice, a carrot top, a potato piece with an eye, a potato piece without an eye and a garlic clove.
setup.caption: 1. Put six pieces in shallow water: onion base, onion middle, carrot top, potato with an eye, potato without, garlic.

setup.art: An onion base in a saucer with green leaves growing up from its centre and white roots below.
setup.caption: 2. Watch where new growth starts on each piece.

setup.art: A child's notebook with two drawings of each piece, day 1 and day 10, and the growing place circled in red.
setup.caption: 3. On day 10, mark with a paper slip where each piece grew.

flow.do: 1. A grown-up cuts the bottom 2 centimetres off the onion, with the root plate. 2. Cut a slice from the onion's middle. 3. Cut the top 2 centimetres off the carrot. 4. Cut two potato pieces, one with an eye and one with plain skin. 5. Add one whole garlic clove. 6. Ask which pieces will regrow, and why. 7. Stand all six pieces in water half a centimetre deep, at a bright window.
flow.say: Here are six pieces. Which ones will grow again, and which will not? Why do you think so?
flow.kid: Look at the six pieces. Guess which will grow again. Say why. Stand them in shallow water.
flow.parent: Stand the garlic clove with the flat end down. Keep the water shallow, so the pieces do not rot. Choose a potato whose eyes have begun to swell, or the potato pieces will need two or three weeks.
flow.context: This is day 1 of Kitchen Regrowers. Here you cut six vegetable pieces and guess which will regrow.

flow.do: 1. On day 4 and day 7, change the water. 2. Look for new green, white or purple growth. 3. Note where it starts on each piece. 4. On day 7, measure the longest shoot and root.
flow.say: Where exactly is the new growth coming from? The cut face, the skin, or one special place?
flow.kid: Change the water. Find the new growth. Where does it start? Show your grown-up.

ask.q: The onion base regrows from its centre and the middle slice does not. What does the base have?
good: The base has the growing point, at the flat plate where the roots join.
The middle slice is only leaf, with no growing point.

flow.wait: Do this on day 4 and day 7
flow.parent: The onion base and the garlic usually show green within three or four days. The carrot top grows new leaves, but not a new carrot. Throw out any piece that goes slimy, and note it down.
flow.context: This step of Kitchen Regrowers is the checking on day 4 and day 7. Here you find where the new growth starts.

flow.do: 1. On day 10, lay the pieces in a row. 2. Put a small paper slip beside the growing place on each. 3. Ask what the growing places have in common. 4. Compare with the Pudina Pieces Test, if you have done it.
flow.say: Look at all the marked places. What did the pieces that stayed the same lack?
flow.kid: Mark where each piece grew with a paper slip. Compare the places.

ask.q: What do the regrowing pieces all have?
good: A bud or growing point: the onion's centre, the potato's eye, the top of the carrot.
Cells that can still divide.

flow.parent: Every regrowing piece has a bud. The onion's bud is in the centre of the base, the carrot's is at the top, and the potato's eye is a bud. The onion slice and the plain potato piece have none.

check.q: A potato piece with an 'eye' sprouts, and a piece with plain skin does not. Why?
options: The eye is a bud with cells that still divide
The plain piece had less water
Potato skin stops growth
check.why: An eye is a bud, and a bud holds cells that can still divide. The plain piece is storage cells only. Both pieces had the same water, and both had skin, so those cannot be the reason.

flow.context: This is the last day of Kitchen Regrowers. Here you compare the pieces and say where the dividing cells were.

challenges.title: Blind Share: share eight pairs with no mistakes, without looking
challenges.context: This is a design challenge. A dividing cell must send one chromosome of every pair to each side, and she has no eyes to check with. Here you must share eight pairs of slips between two bags while blindfolded, with no mistakes.
challenges.problem: Sixteen paper slips are numbered 1 to 8 twice. Blindfolded, share them between two bags so that each bag gets exactly one of every number. Your method must work three times in a row.
constraints: The sharer wears a blindfold from the moment the sharing starts.
You may prepare the slips in any way before the blindfold goes on.
A helper may speak, but may not touch the slips.
materials: two cloth bags or two katoris
paper clips, clothes pegs or thread
general: Clip each pair together before the blindfold goes on. Then unclip one pair at a time and drop one slip in each bag.
Lay the pairs in a row down the middle of the table. Slide one slip of each pair to the left and one to the right.
creative: Tie a thread to each slip of a pair. Two people pull from opposite sides of the table. A pair that is tied to only one side shows up at once, because it does not come apart.
Give the helper one job: to say 'go' only when every pair is held from both sides. This is a checkpoint.
Fold each pair together so that fingers can feel a thick double slip and never mistake one slip for a pair.
challenges.your_turn: Now design your own method. Test it three times and count the mistakes. Which idea does your method share with a dividing cell: holding pairs together, lining them up, pulling from both sides, or a checkpoint?

setup.art: Sixteen numbered paper slips on a table, clipped into eight matching pairs, with two cloth bags at the left and right edges.
setup.caption: 1. Number 16 slips 1 to 8 twice. Prepare them any way you like.

setup.art: A blindfolded child sliding one slip of a clipped pair to the left bag and the other to the right bag, while a helper watches.
setup.caption: 2. Put on the blindfold and share one of every number into each bag.

flow.do: 1. Make the 16 slips. 2. Mix them in a heap. 3. Your child puts on the blindfold and shares the heap into two bags, eight in each. 4. Tip out the bags and count the mistakes.
flow.say: First try it with no method at all. Eight slips in each bag. Then we count how many numbers went wrong.
flow.kid: Mix the slips. Put on the blindfold. Put eight in each bag. Count the mistakes.
flow.parent: A mistake is a number that is twice in one bag and missing from the other. A blind share from a heap nearly always has several.
flow.context: This is the first step of Blind Share. Here you share the slips with no method, to see how many mistakes that makes.

flow.do: 1. Offer two starting ideas: clip each pair together, or lay the slips in a row. 2. Your child chooses one and says why it should work. 3. Test it three times, blindfolded. 4. Count the mistakes each time.
flow.say: Which idea do you want to test first? Why should it stop the mistakes? Try it three times.
flow.kid: Pick one idea. Say why it should work. Test it three times. Count the mistakes.

ask.q: Why does holding each pair together until the last moment help?
good: You always know which two slips are partners.
You only have to send one each way, and you can feel that.

flow.context: This step of Blind Share tests one of the usual ideas.

flow.do: 1. Your child designs a new method, or improves the first. 2. Test it three times. 3. Read how a cell does it: copies stay joined, thin threads from both sides take hold, a checkpoint waits until all are held, then the join is cut. 4. Ask which parts the two methods share.
flow.say: Now I will read how a cell shares her chromosomes. Then we will see which parts your method shares with her.
flow.kid: Design your own method. Test it three times.

ask.q: A cell waits until every chromosome is held from both sides. Which part of your method does the same job?
good: The helper who says 'go'.
Checking that every pair is clipped before starting.

flow.parent: A real cell uses all four ideas. The copies are held together, they line up in the middle, threads pull from both sides, and a checkpoint stops everything until each one is attached.
flow.context: This is the last step of Blind Share. Here you test your own method and compare it with a dividing cell.

worksheets.title: Mitosis, meiosis, stem cells and planned cell death (core)

items.p: Which kind of division makes two cells with the same full set of chromosomes?
items.why: Mitosis copies every chromosome and divides once, so both cells have the full set. Meiosis halves the set. Fertilisation joins two cells, and crossing over is a swap of pieces.

items.p: A human body cell has 46 chromosomes. How many does a human egg cell have?
items.why: An egg cell has half the set, one chromosome from each of the 23 pairs. Choosing 46 forgets that the sperm cell brings 23 more.

items.p: True or false: meiosis happens in every part of the body.
items.why: False. Meiosis happens only in the organs that make egg cells or sperm cells. Everywhere else, cells divide by mitosis.

items.p: In meiosis the cell copies the chromosomes once and then divides ____ times.
items.why: One copying and two divisions give four cells with half the chromosomes each. One division would give two cells with the full set, which is mitosis.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
items.why: These five words are used all through the unit. A strong answer could give an example of each.
pairs: Mitosis
division that makes two cells with the full set
Meiosis
division that makes sex cells with half the set
Stem cell
a cell that has not taken a job yet
Fertilisation
an egg cell and a sperm cell joining
Programmed cell death
a cell taking herself apart by plan

items.p: Sort these cells by the kind of division that made them.
items.why: Body cells for growing and mending come from mitosis. Sex cells, and the young pollen grains of a flower, come from meiosis.
items: a cell at a root tip

items.p: What can a stem cell do that a red blood cell cannot?
opts: Divide and make other kinds of cell
items.why: A stem cell can divide, and her daughters can specialise. A red blood cell is fully specialised and never divides. Carrying oxygen is the red cell's own job.

items.p: True or false: a blood stem cell in a grown-up can make new nerve cells.
items.why: False. An adult stem cell makes only the cells of her own tissue. A blood stem cell makes blood cells. Only the stem cells of a very young embryo can make every kind.

items.p: How did your fingers become separate before you were born?
opts: The cells between them died by plan
Each finger was added one by one
The bones cut through the skin
items.why: The hand begins as a paddle. The cells between the finger bones die by plan and are cleared away. Nothing tears, and nothing is hurt.

items.p: The death of cells by injury, such as a burn, is called ____.
items.why: In necrosis the cells swell and burst, and the place becomes sore. Apoptosis is the planned, tidy kind of cell death.

items.p: Put the steps of planned cell death in order.
a: The cell gets a signal, or senses damage inside herself
The cell shrinks and cuts up her own DNA
She packs herself into small sealed parcels
items.why: The signal comes first, then the tidy taking apart, then the clearing up. Nothing spills at any step.
items: She packs herself into small sealed parcels
The cell gets a signal, or senses damage inside herself
The cell shrinks and cuts up her own DNA

items.p: In the Pudina Pieces Test, a bare node grew roots and a leaf alone did not. What does that show?
items.a: It shows that the cells that can make new roots are at the node. The bare node had no leaves and still made roots, so leaves are not what makes roots. The leaf had no node and made none.
items.why: A strong answer uses both pieces: the node without a leaf, and the leaf without a node.

items.p: Why does the Pudina Pieces Test use five pieces of each kind, and not one?
opts: One piece could fail by bad luck
items.why: A single piece can rot or dry out for reasons that have nothing to do with nodes. If four or five of a kind do the same thing, the result can be trusted.

items.p: Name two things in your home made of cells that died by plan. Say what job the dead cells did.
items.a: For example: a wooden spoon and a cotton towel. Wood is made of a tree's dead, hollow water pipes and stiff fibres, which carried water and held the tree up. Hair, nails, coir, wool and feathers are also right.
items.why: A strong answer names the living being the thing came from, and says what the dead cells did there.

items.p: Draw a cell with 4 chromosomes. Then draw the two cells she makes by mitosis.
items.a: One cell with 4 chromosomes, and two cells below it that each have the same 4 chromosomes.
items.why: A strong drawing gives each new cell all 4 chromosomes. A drawing with 2 in each cell shows a mix-up with meiosis.
items.art: A large empty circle at the top of the page with two empty circles below it, joined by arrows.

worksheets.title: Halving, shuffling and cells that can still divide (stretch)

items.p: Why do matching chromosomes line up as partners in meiosis?
opts: So each new cell gets one of every pair
So the DNA is copied again
items.why: When partners line up together and then separate, each side gets one of every pair. Without the pairing, a cell could get two of one kind and none of another.

items.p: A rice plant has 24 chromosomes in each body cell. How many are in a rice egg cell?
items.why: A sex cell has half the set. 24 ÷ 2 = 12. A rice sperm cell brings 12 more, so the new seed has 24 again.

items.p: A cell has 5 pairs of chromosomes. How many different sex cells can the shuffle make?
items.why: Each pair doubles the number. 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 = 32. Answering 10 comes from adding 2 for each pair, when each pair doubles it.

items.p: The swap of matching pieces between two partner chromosomes is called ____ ____.
items.why: Crossing over happens early in meiosis. After it, one chromosome carries a mix of the two partners.

items.p: True or false: two sisters with the same parents always have exactly the same chromosomes.
items.why: False. Each sister grew from a different egg cell and a different sperm cell, and each of those had a different mix. Only identical twins start with the same set.

items.p: Three of these are made by mitosis. Which one is made by meiosis?
items.why: A sperm cell has half the chromosomes, so meiosis makes it. Skin, liver and root tip cells are body cells with the full set.

items.p: Sort each fact: is it about embryonic stem cells or adult stem cells?
items.why: Embryonic stem cells are in an embryo a few days old and can make every kind of body cell. Adult stem cells stay in a formed body and make only the cells of their own tissue.
items: can make every kind of body cell
is in an embryo a few days old
remakes the gut lining every few days

items.p: A pea plant has 14 chromosomes. Explain what would happen over three generations with no meiosis.
items.a: Each parent would give all 14, so the child would have 28. The grandchild would have 56 and the next generation 112. The number would double every time. Meiosis halves it to 7 first, so 7 and 7 make 14 again.
items.why: A strong answer shows the doubling with numbers, and says that halving before joining keeps the number steady.

items.p: A duck has webbed feet and a hen does not. Explain the difference using planned cell death.
items.a: Both embryos start with paddle-shaped feet. In the hen, the cells between the toes die by plan, so the toes separate. In the duck, a signal blocks that death, so the cells stay and form the web.
items.why: A strong answer says that both start the same, and that the difference is whether the cells between the toes die.

items.p: Draw a pudina cutting standing in water. Label a node, a leaf, a new root and the water line.
a: Node: where the leaves join the stem
New root: growing out at a node under the water
items.why: A strong drawing has the roots coming from a node, not from the cut end or from the bare stem between nodes.
items.art: A blank tumbler outline with space to draw a cutting inside it, and four blank label lines.

items.p: Three people talk about a cell that dies by plan.
items.a: A strong answer uses two examples, such as fingers, a tadpole's tail, sunburn or cancer. It chooses one view, and says what one of the others has right.
items.why: The doctor is right about injury and illness. The biologist is right that bodies are built and kept safe by planned death. The third view asks a real question that science has not settled.

views.who: A doctor in a burns ward
views.says: Cell death is what I fight every day. My work is to keep cells alive.
Without cells dying on time, you would have no fingers and many more cancers.
The cell got a signal and obeyed. Is that giving, or just following orders?

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? Use two examples from this lesson. Then say what one of the others has right.

items.p: Put the steps of meiosis in order.
a: Partners line up side by side and swap pieces
The first division separates the partners
The second division separates the copies
items.why: Copying comes first. Then the partners pair up and cross over. The first division parts the partners, and the second parts the copies.
items: The first division separates the partners
The second division separates the copies
Partners line up side by side and swap pieces

items.p: Which of these is one cause of cancer?
opts: Damaged cells that fail to die
items.why: A cell with damaged instructions normally takes herself apart. If she does not, and keeps dividing, a cancer can start. Too much planned death causes other problems, not cancer.

items.p: Which stem cell treatment is well proven?
opts: A bone marrow transplant for blood cancer
An injection that cures any illness
items.why: Bone marrow transplants have worked for decades. The other three are not possible today, and anyone who offers them is selling something unproven.

items.p: A pudina piece cut from between two nodes grows one root. What should you check first?
opts: Whether a node is hidden at one end
Whether the water was too cold
Whether the piece was green enough
items.why: An odd result deserves a second look before you change your idea. A node at the very end of the piece is the most likely cause.

worksheets.title: Mistakes, going back and open questions (challenge)

items.p: A woman of 30 releases an egg cell. When did that egg cell begin meiosis?
items.why: All of a girl's egg cells begin meiosis before she is born and then pause. This one waited for more than 30 years.

items.p: A tiny roundworm makes 1,090 body cells, and 131 of them die by plan. How many are left?
items.why: 1,090 − 131 = 959. Every worm of this kind ends with the same 959 cells, which showed that the deaths are planned.

items.p: Bone marrow makes about 2 million red blood cells each second. How many million is that in one minute?
items.why: There are 60 seconds in a minute. 2 × 60 = 120. So about 120 million red blood cells are made every minute.

items.p: A fertilised egg has 47 chromosomes, not 46. Explain how meiosis could have caused this.
items.a: In meiosis, the two partners of one pair went to the same side when they should have separated. That egg or sperm cell had 24 chromosomes. When it joined a normal sex cell with 23, the total was 47.
items.why: A strong answer says that one pair failed to separate, and shows the sum 24 + 23 = 47.

items.p: Plant cells go back to dividing more easily than animal cells. Give one piece of evidence for each.
items.a: Plants: a pudina cutting grows new roots from a node, and whole carrot plants have been grown from single root cells. Animals: a human does not regrow an arm, and scientists had to switch on four genes to turn skin cells into stem-like cells.
items.why: A strong answer gives a real observation for each side, not only the claim.

items.p: Plan a fair test: does a money plant cutting need a node to grow roots?
items.a: Cut several pieces with a node and several with no node, all from the same plant on the same day. Give them the same water, light and time. Count how many of each kind grow roots after two or three weeks.
items.why: A strong plan changes only one thing, the node. It keeps everything else the same and uses several pieces of each kind.

items.p: Three biologists talk about why most animals have two parents.
items.a: A strong answer uses evidence: rotifers that have copied themselves for millions of years, snails that use two parents more where parasites are common, or the 8 million mixes from the shuffle. It chooses one view and gives a fair point from another.
items.why: This is a real, unsettled question. Each view fits some living beings well and others badly.

views.says: Copying is better. A mother who copies herself passes on all her instructions.
Shuffling is better. Children who are all different are harder for germs to beat.
Neither is better. It depends on where and how a living being lives.

items.ask: Whose view do you agree with most? Give one piece of evidence. Then say what one of the others has right.

items.p: Draw two partner chromosomes before and after crossing over. Use two colours.
items.a: Before: one chromosome all in the first colour and one all in the second. After: each chromosome mostly its own colour, with a matching piece of the other colour.
items.why: A strong drawing swaps pieces of the same length from the same place. The chromosomes stay the same length as before.
items.art: Two pairs of blank chromosome outlines, labelled 'before' and 'after'.

items.p: True or false: you got exactly one quarter of your DNA from each grandparent.
items.why: False. A quarter is the average. Because of the shuffle and crossing over, you may have a little more from one grandparent and a little less from another.

items.p: Match each cause to what it leads to.
items.why: Each pair links a step in a cell's life to what happens when that step changes.
pairs: Damaged cells fail to die
cells pile up, as in a cancer
Partners fail to separate in meiosis
a sex cell with an extra chromosome
Bone marrow loses its stem cells
no new blood cells are made
A death signal is blocked between the toes
webbed feet
A cut stem's node cells start dividing
new roots grow

items.p: Three of these die by plan. Which one dies by injury?
items.why: Skin under a bad burn is killed by heat, which is necrosis. The other three die on time as part of normal growing.
opts: Skin cells under a bad burn

items.p: Scientists turned mouse skin cells back into ____ cells by switching on four genes.
items.why: This showed that a specialised cell still holds the instructions for other jobs. They are closed, not lost.

items.p: Why is a gecko's regrown tail called a repair and not a copy?
opts: It has a cartilage rod, not new bones
It is a different animal's tail
It is made of plant cells
items.why: The first tail has a row of small bones. The new tail has a single rod of cartilage, the bendy material in your ear. It works, but it is not the same as the first.

items.p: A human has 23 pairs of chromosomes. About how many different egg cells can the shuffle make?
items.why: Each pair doubles the number, and doubling 23 times gives 8,388,608. Answering 46 comes from adding 2 for each pair, when each pair doubles it.

items.p: Old yeast cells sometimes die in a tidy, programmed way. Why do they do it?
opts: It is proved to feed the colony
items.why: Some biologists say the death helps the yeast cell's sisters. Others say it may be a side effect of other machinery. The question is still open.

quiz.p: A scraped elbow heals. Which kind of division makes the new skin cells?
quiz.why: Healing needs more skin cells of the same kind, with the full set of chromosomes. That is mitosis. Meiosis only makes sex cells.

quiz.p: In the simple picture, how many cells does one cell make by meiosis?
quiz.why: Meiosis is one copying and two divisions, so one cell becomes four. Answering 2 is a mix-up with mitosis.

quiz.p: A dog's body cells have 78 chromosomes. How many are in a dog's sperm cell?
quiz.why: A sex cell has half the set. 78 ÷ 2 = 39. The number 23 is right for humans only.

quiz.p: Why are a brother and a sister from the same parents not copies of each other?
opts: Each grew from a different egg and sperm
quiz.why: Meiosis gives every egg cell and every sperm cell a different mix of chromosomes. Food and age change a body, but they do not change which chromosomes it started with.

quiz.p: Which cells can become every kind of cell in the body?
opts: Stem cells of an embryo a few days old
quiz.why: Only the stem cells of a very young embryo can make every kind. Blood and skin stem cells make only their own tissue, and red blood cells do not divide at all.

quiz.p: True or false: your bone marrow makes new blood cells every second.
quiz.why: True. Blood stem cells in the marrow make about two million red blood cells each second, to replace those that wear out.

quiz.p: Which of these is planned cell death?
opts: Skin burnt by a hot pan
quiz.why: The tail cells die on a signal and are reused. Burning, crushing and freezing kill cells by injury, which is necrosis.

quiz.p: How is planned cell death different from death by injury?
opts: The cell packs herself up and nothing spills
quiz.why: In planned death the cell shrinks into sealed parcels, and cleaner cells remove them. A burst cell that spills and causes soreness is the sign of injury.

quiz.p: Roots grew at the node of a pudina piece and not between nodes. What is at the node?
opts: Cells that can start dividing again
quiz.why: A node holds a bud and cells that can go back to dividing. The stem between the nodes is finished, and makes no new parts.

quiz.p: Three pairs of chromosomes can be shuffled into 8 different sex cells. How many for four pairs?
quiz.why: Each extra pair doubles the number, and 8 × 2 = 16. Answering 10 comes from adding 2.

quiz.p: Why do most animals have two parents, when copying looks simpler?
opts: There is a leading idea, still debated
quiz.why: The leading idea is that shuffled children are harder for germs to beat. But some animals copy themselves very well, so scientists still debate it.

applications: Bone marrow transplants give a person with a blood cancer a new supply of blood stem cells from a healthy donor.
Eye doctors repair a chemical burn of the cornea by growing new surface from stem cells taken at the edge of the person's other eye.
Gardeners and farmers grow new plants from cuttings. Sugarcane, tapioca, money plant, rose and hibiscus are all planted as pieces of stem with a node.
Tissue culture laboratories grow thousands of banana and orchid plants from small groups of cells, so that farmers get plants free of disease.
Many cancer medicines work by pushing cancer cells to die by plan, as healthy damaged cells would have done.
Plant breeders use the shuffle of meiosis. They cross two rice varieties and search among the mixed grandchildren for a plant with the best of both.
Doctors can count the chromosomes of a baby before birth, to see whether the sharing in meiosis left one too many or one too few.

open_questions.q: Why can a flatworm or a salamander regrow lost parts, when a human cannot regrow an arm?
open_questions.why_open: Humans have many of the same genes, and small children can even regrow a fingertip. Nobody yet knows why the rest of this ability is switched off in us.

open_questions.q: Can stem cells be used to repair a damaged heart, spinal cord or brain?
open_questions.why_open: It works in some animal tests, and trials in people are going on. So far the results in people are small or mixed, and making the new cells join up correctly is hard.

open_questions.q: Why did meiosis and two parents begin at all?
open_questions.why_open: Copying passes on all of a mother's instructions and needs no partner. The idea that the shuffle keeps ahead of germs has some evidence, but it does not explain every case.

open_questions.q: Why do single-celled beings such as yeast have a programmed way of dying?
open_questions.why_open: It may protect their sister cells, or it may be a side effect of other machinery. Experiments have not yet settled it.

open_questions.q: How does an egg cell stay healthy while paused in meiosis for forty years?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists know that the links between the paired chromosomes weaken with time. They do not know how the cell protects everything else for so long.

open_questions.q: Can working egg and sperm cells be made from skin cells?
open_questions.why_open: In 2016 Katsuhiko Hayashi's team in Japan did it in mice, and healthy pups were born. Nobody has done it with human cells, and people disagree about whether anyone should.

maths.problem: In the Shuffle Test, 3 pairs of chromosomes gave 8 possible egg cells, and 4 pairs gave 16. How many are possible with 6 pairs? What is the rule?
maths.answer: 64. Each extra pair doubles the number.
maths.explain: 3 pairs give 8 and 4 pairs give 16. Double again for 5 pairs: 32. Double again for 6 pairs: 64. Every result so far can be followed by either chromosome of the new pair, so the number doubles each time.
maths.context: This is about the Shuffle Test. Coins stand for pairs of chromosomes, and each toss makes one egg cell.
maths.why_maths: Once you see the doubling rule, you can find the number for any living being without tossing coins for days.

maths.problem: A pea plant has 14 chromosomes. Suppose nothing were halved, so the number doubled in every generation. How many chromosomes would a plant have after 5 generations?
maths.explain: Double five times: 14, 28, 56, 112, 224, 448. That is 14 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2, or 14 × 32. No cell could manage a set that keeps doubling, which is why meiosis halves the number first.
maths.context: This is about Double Trouble. Seeds stand for a pea plant's chromosomes, and you pass them on with no halving.
maths.why_maths: Working out the doubling shows how quickly the number runs away. That tells you why halving is needed, not just that it happens.

maths.problem: In a Pudina Pieces Test, 5 of 5 leafy node pieces and 4 of 5 bare node pieces grew roots. None of the 10 pieces with no node did. What percentage of node pieces rooted? One node piece failed. Does that change the conclusion?
maths.answer: 90 percent of the node pieces rooted, and 0 percent of the others. The one failure does not change the conclusion.
maths.explain: 9 of the 10 node pieces rooted. 9 ÷ 10 = 0.9, which is 90 percent. None of the 10 pieces with no node rooted. One piece can fail from rot or a bad cut. The gap between 90 percent and 0 percent is far too big to be luck.
maths.context: This is about the Pudina Pieces Test. Four kinds of pudina pieces stand in water, and you count how many of each kind grow roots.

chart.title: Made-up results on day 9: pieces with roots

maths.why_maths: A percentage lets you compare two groups fairly. It also helps you judge whether one odd piece matters.

maths.problem: In the Shuffle Test, three coins can fall in 8 ways. In 24 tosses, how many times would you expect each way? A family got MMM 6 times. Are their coins unfair?
maths.answer: About 3 times each. Six times is not enough to call the coins unfair.
maths.explain: 24 ÷ 8 = 3, so each result is expected about 3 times. But chance is lumpy. In only 24 tosses, one result often comes up 5 or 6 times and another only once. To test the coins properly, the family would need hundreds of tosses.
maths.context: This is about the Shuffle Test. Three coins are tossed 24 times, and each toss stands for one egg cell.
maths.why_maths: Knowing what chance alone can do stops you from seeing a pattern where there is none.

maths.problem: A cell has 2 pairs of chromosomes. List every different egg cell the shuffle can make. If a father can make as many kinds of sperm, how many different fertilised eggs are possible?
maths.answer: 4 kinds of egg cell, and 16 different fertilised eggs.
maths.explain: Call the pairs M or F. The egg cells are MM, MF, FM and FF, which is 4. Each of the 4 egg cells can join any of the 4 kinds of sperm. 4 × 4 = 16. For humans the same sum is about 8 million × 8 million, which is more than 70 trillion.
maths.context: This is about the Shuffle Test, where coins stand for pairs of chromosomes. Here you count the egg cells and then bring in the father.
maths.why_maths: Listing in a careful order makes sure no possibility is missed. Multiplying then counts the pairs without drawing every one.

maths.problem: The longest root on a pudina piece was 4 millimetres on day 5, 12 millimetres on day 7 and 20 millimetres on day 9. How fast is it growing? How long will it be on day 11 if it carries on?
maths.answer: 4 millimetres a day. About 28 millimetres on day 11.
maths.explain: From day 5 to day 7 the root grew 8 millimetres, and from day 7 to day 9 another 8. That is 8 millimetres in 2 days, or 4 millimetres a day. Two more days add 8, so 20 + 8 = 28 millimetres. A real root may speed up or slow down, so this is a prediction to check.
maths.context: This is about the Pudina Pieces Test. On each check day you measure the longest new root with a ruler.

chart.title: Made-up example: the longest root on one pudina piece

maths.why_maths: A steady rate lets you predict a measurement before you take it. Checking the prediction tells you whether the growth is really steady.
