how_we_found_out.context: How did people find out that cells can die by plan? This card tells the true story, and the idea that turned out wrong.
how_we_found_out.story: For a long time, scientists thought a cell died only when something harmed her. In 1842 Carl Vogt, working in Switzerland, watched toad tadpoles change and saw healthy cells disappear as new parts formed. Few people took notice. In 1949 Viktor Hamburger and Rita Levi-Montalcini counted nerve cells in chick embryos, and found that many died as a normal part of growing. In 1972, in Aberdeen, John Kerr, Andrew Wyllie and Alastair Currie described a tidy kind of cell death that looked the same in many tissues. They named it apoptosis, a Greek word for leaves falling from a tree. The proof that it is planned came from a roundworm one millimetre long. In Cambridge, John Sulston watched every cell of the worm divide, through a microscope, for years. The same 131 cells died in every worm, at the same moments. Then Hilary Ellis and Robert Horvitz found genes for dying. In worms with one of those genes broken, the 131 cells lived.
how_we_found_out.who: Carl Vogt. Viktor Hamburger and Rita Levi-Montalcini. John Kerr, Andrew Wyllie and Alastair Currie. John Sulston. Hilary Ellis and Robert Horvitz.
how_we_found_out.when: 1842 (Vogt), 1949 (Hamburger and Levi-Montalcini), 1972 (the name apoptosis), 1977 to 1983 (Sulston's cell maps) and 1986 (the genes)
how_we_found_out.wrong_idea: That a cell dies only by accident, when something harms her. Sulston's worms showed that the same cells die at the same moments in every animal. Ellis and Horvitz showed that the cells need working genes in order to die.
how_we_found_out.art: A scientist at a microscope drawing a branching map of cell divisions, with some branch ends marked by a small cross, beside a tiny curved roundworm.

roots.context: We have learned that cells divide in two ways, that some cells have no job yet, and that some cells die by plan. Now we ask what this tells us about ourselves and the world.

deep_truth.truth: In Paddle to Hand, the dough hand that held together was made by cutting dough away. Your real fingers were freed the same way, when the cells between them died on time. A frog's legs are finished with material from the dying tail. So in a living body, cells dying at the right time is part of growing, not a failure of it.
deep_truth.habit: We think of death as the opposite of life, something that only happens when life fails. Cells show that planned dying is one of the ways a body is built and kept safe. Too little of it gives webbed fingers and cancers.
deep_truth.evidence: In Paddle to Hand, fingers came from taking away. In the Dead on Purpose Hunt, hair, nails, wood and cotton were all cells that finished their work by dying. In a roundworm, the same 131 cells die in every worm, and those cells need working genes in order to die.

three.who_am_i: The egg cell that became you began to form inside your mother before she was born. Your hand has fingers because some of your own cells died on time.
three.what_is_life: Life carries on in two ways at once. Mitosis copies what works. Meiosis shuffles it into someone who has never lived before.
three.what_is_this_world: In the living world, ending is part of making. A tree's water pipes, a frog's legs and your fingers all needed some cells to finish.

roots.thread: One fertilised egg becomes trillions of cells by mitosis. The cells take hundreds of different jobs, and some die so that the others can form a hand or stay safe. Then meiosis makes single cells again, each a new mix, and one of them may begin another body. So a body is one cell that became many, and the many still act together as one.

teachings.teaching: Clay is shaped into a pot, and the empty space inside is what makes the pot useful. Doors and windows are cut in a wall, and the openings are what make the room useful.
teachings.link: The gaps between your fingers are what make a hand useful. The emptiness inside a tree's dead pipe cells is what carries the water. In both, something was taken away by plan.

teachings.teaching: Thiruvalluvar says that death is like falling asleep, and birth is like waking from that sleep.
teachings.link: The verse puts dying and being born side by side, as two halves of one rhythm. In your body, millions of cells reach their end every second and millions are made. Both belong to being alive.

teachings.teaching: For one who is born, death is certain. For one who has died, birth is certain.
teachings.link: A gut lining cell is born, works for a few days and dies, and a new one takes her place. The gut carries on because both things keep happening.

science.text: Every cell weighs signals to live against signals to die before she acts. Biologists call this a cell fate decision, and they can measure the signals.
In animal cells, one main death signal is let out by the mitochondria, which were once free-living bacteria. Why the switch for death sits there is not known.

other_view.view: Apoptosis is a chain of chemical reactions, in which certain proteins cut up other proteins. Words such as 'decides' or 'for the body' are only a way of speaking. Cells that carried this chain left more descendants, and that is the whole explanation.

practice.title: Look at the gaps
practice.say: Hold one hand up against the light and spread your fingers. Look at the four gaps, not at the fingers. Each gap was once full of living cells. Close your fingers slowly, then open them again. Breathe in as they open, and out as they close. Do this five times. Now find the small web at the base of two fingers. What do you notice?
practice.kid: Hold your hand up to the light. Spread your fingers. Look at the gaps. Cells once filled each gap. Open and close your hand five times. Breathe in as it opens. Breathe out as it closes.

ask: The cells between your fingers died so that your hand could form. Were they you?
A tadpole's tail becomes part of the frog's legs. Did the tail end, or did it change?
If dying on time is part of how a body is built, is death the opposite of life?
The egg cell that became you waited inside your mother from before her birth. Where does one life stop and the next begin?

playtest: The experiments and activities in this lesson were reasoned through step by step. They have not yet been tried at home, so please treat times and amounts as a starting point. The Pudina Pieces Test (core) needs a fresh bunch of pudina with firm stems, a tumbler and three katoris, and it runs for nine days. Pudina usually shows white root bumps at the nodes in three to five days in warm weather, and takes up to twelve days in a cool room. The between-node pieces are short and may rot, so the water must be shallow and changed every two days. A slimy piece is thrown out and written down as a result. If a between-node piece roots, look for a node hidden at one end. Money plant or karpooravalli can be used if there is no pudina, but money plant takes two to three weeks. Paddle to Hand (core) needs only atta dough and an ice cream stick. The Shuffle Test needs four different coins, and most families see 7 or 8 of the 8 results in 24 tosses. In Double Trouble, a random pick of seven slips nearly always misses a number, but about 1 pick in 27 does not, so the step says to pick again. Two Dances needs eight paper strips and paper clips, and a coin for the chance sharing. Kitchen Regrowers needs a grown-up for the knife, and a potato whose eyes have begun to swell, or the potato needs two to three weeks. Blind Share needs two people. The card game has 24 cards and works for one player against the pile. No part needs a garden.
